title: ASCG: Adaptive Spatial Classifier Guidance for Surgical Concept Suppression in Diffusion Models
summary: While text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models achieve remarkable quality, they risk producing harmful content. Existing safety mechanisms often rely on indiscriminate, global interventions that induce unintended semantic drift and degrade image quality. To address this, we propose Adaptive Spatial Classifier Guidance (ASCG), a necessity-driven framework that employs probabilistic monitoring to activate guidance selectively upon harm detection. By leveraging Grad-CAM for localized suppression, ASCG effectively removes harmful concepts while preserving superior semantic fidelity compared to conventional methods. Furthermore, we overcome the limitations of traditional metrics like NudeNet---which fails to assess semantic integrity---by introducing a VLM-based evaluation framework to provide a fine-grained, robust analysis of both safety and context preservation. Our results demonstrate that ASCG not only balances safety and fidelity but also exhibits remarkable plug-and-play synergy with existing frameworks to establish state-of-the-art performance.

title: Accelerate Bench: Evaluating Agents for Application-Level Program Optimization
summary: Application optimization requires coding agents to discover useful changes and coordinate them across a complete program while preserving the required computation. We introduce Accelerate Bench, a benchmark of 32 CPU optimization tasks adapted from scientific applications and supercomputing competitions. Each task provides a working program and specifies the workload, correctness requirements, timing boundaries, and permitted edits, leaving agents to choose where and how to optimize. Public testing supports iterative development, and a separate verifier scores the final submission. On benchmark version 1.1, we evaluate 16 coding agents, each pairing a model with a harness. Their Score@1 ranges from 25.5% to 67.4%. Most of their programs are correct, and the size of the speedup separates them: the two leading agents are at least 2x faster on 22 or more of the 32 tasks, while the other fourteen reach 2x on 8 to 17 and leave 125 of their 412 correct outcomes below 1.25x. Controlled replays show why coordination across an application matters: identical source code runs between 0.29x and 2.12x depending only on build and runtime settings, and one code change is worth 1.01x or 6.4x depending on another. Accelerate Bench pairs executable workloads with agents' programs and trajectories to evaluate both their gains and the process behind them.

title: AdMem: Expectation-Grounded Procedural Memory for Long-Horizon Task-Solving Agents
summary: An agent that carries memory across tasks is only as good as the entries it keeps. We begin from an observation that is easy to reproduce and uncomfortable for the field: naively accumulating cross-task experience can make an agent \emph{worse} than one with no memory at all. On AgentBoard, a workflow-induction memory solves fewer tasks than a memoryless ReAct agent in seven of eight domains, and a per-step procedural store with no surrounding structure loses half of ReAct's completions on Jericho. We argue that the missing ingredients are per-action credit assignment and an explicit life cycle for stored entries, and present AdMem, which supplies both. Before each action the actor commits to an expected outcome; a concurrently running critic scores the realized outcome against that expectation and writes a procedural entry carrying a binary reward and a reflection, so credit lands on the action that earned it and no environment reward is required. Each entry then carries a scalar utility, updated online under a noisy-OR reward model, that ranks retrieval jointly with context similarity and drives eviction and merging, giving the store a forgetting and consolidation policy instead of unbounded growth. Across 707 tasks in eight AgentBoard domains AdMem solves 441 against 388 for ReAct and 312 for the workflow-induction baseline --- a pooled gain significant under a two-sided Fisher exact test, concentrated in the domains that supply transferable cross-task structure. All memory stays human-readable text, which is what makes the failures above diagnosable --- and, as we discuss, also makes the store an auditable but attackable surface.

title: AdaFlowLite: Scalable and Non-blocking Inference on Asynchronous Mobile Data
summary:
The rise of mobile devices equipped with numerous sensors, such as LiDAR and cameras, has driven the adoption of multi-modal deep intelligence for distributed sensing tasks, such as smart cabins and driving assistance. However, the arrival time of mobile sensory data vary due to modality size and network dynamics, which can lead to delays (if waiting for slow data) or accuracy decline (if inference proceeds without waiting). Moreover, the diversity and dynamic nature of mobile systems exacerbate this challenge. In response, we present a shift to \textit{opportunistic} inference for asynchronous distributed multi-modal data, enabling inference as soon as partial data arrives. While existing methods focus on optimizing modality consistency and complementarity, known as modal affinity, they lack a \textit{computational} approach to control this affinity in open-world mobile environments. %
\sysname pioneers the formulation of structured cross-modality affinity in mobile contexts using a hierarchical analysis-based normalized matrix. This approach accommodates the diversity and dynamics of modalities, generalizing across different types and numbers of inputs. Employing an multi-modal lightweight Swin Transformer (MMLST), \sysname facilitates real-time and flexible data imputation, adapting to various modalities and downstream tasks without retraining. Experiments show that \sysname significantly reduces inference latency by up to 80.4\% and enhances accuracy by up to 62.1\%, while achieving nearly a 50\% reduction in energy consumption, outperforming status quo approaches. Also, this method can enhance LLM performance to preprocess asynchronous data.

title: AdaModalX: Synchronization-Free MFM Inference for Distributed Multimodal Mobile Sensing via Progressive Data Orchestration
summary: Multimodal foundation models (MFMs) support generalizable inference in distributed mobile sensing applications by integrating heterogeneous data streams. However, existing MFM inference pipelines typically require complete and synchronized multimodal inputs, whereas mobile sensing streams arrive asynchronously due to network variability and heterogeneous data volumes across modalities. Waiting for all modalities increases end-to-end latency, while inference with incomplete inputs can reduce accuracy. We argue that multimodal inference should depend on the utility of available information rather than modality completeness. Based on this principle, we propose AdaModalX, a progressive multimodal inference framework that decouples inference execution from modality synchronization through runtime utility-aware orchestration. At each device, importance-aware data uploading uses a lightweight probe distilled from the edge-side MFM to allow reliable samples to exit locally while uncertain samples continue uploading. At the edge, on-demand MFM activation constructs candidates from fully received samples and, when needed, imputed features derived from partially received delayed inputs. A lightweight contribution assessor built on frozen MFM encoders estimates candidate utility and activates the MFM once the candidate meets its corresponding utility threshold. Experiments on four mobile sensing applications show that AdaModalX improves the accuracy-latency trade-off, achieving up to 26.97% accuracy improvement and up to 64.75% end-to-end latency reduction.

title: Advancing Cognitive Pairwise Comparisons for Human-Centric Artificial Intelligence and Data Science: A Human-in-the-Loop Framework
summary: Human-centric artificial intelligence and data science (HCAD) systems increasingly involve human-in-the-loop (HITL) interventions to overcome the limitations of fully automated machine learning algorithms, such as automation bias and the inability to incorporate tacit domain knowledge, and continuously improve predictive performance. Data transformations, feature selection, feature weighting, and model selection usually require laborious human involvement across iterations of artificial intelligence and data science (AI&DS) pipelines, making development a challenging and time-consuming process. The Cognitive Pairwise Comparison (CPC) framework is proposed as a human-centric methodology to elicit preferences and priorities in a structured format. To establish essential facets of human-centricity, this research advances the CPC methodology so that user preference elicitation can be systematically quantified in these challenging AI&DS tasks. To demonstrate the usability and validity of these facets, this study presents several applications within movie recommender systems using the MovieLens dataset. It exemplifies how the extended CPC framework can facilitate interactions between human judgments and data across supervised learning, dimensionality reduction, and unsupervised learning algorithms.

title: Agent-Guided Configuration Tuning for SMT Solvers
summary:
SMT solvers expose many configuration choices that determine how well their existing algorithms perform on a workload. We present, to our knowledge, the first workflow that uses general-purpose LLM agents to tune SMT solver configurations. Agents read solver documentation, source code, and persistent experiment records to propose option changes, and a deterministic harness measures each proposal, validates the returned models, and selects changes separately for each competition Division. Over roughly nine weeks, our tuning campaign recorded 4,545 proposals for cvc5 across 13 Divisions and 36 logics.
  We evaluate the tuned configurations on the 2026 and 2025 SMT-COMP ModelValidation benchmarks under a 24-second cutoff. On problems not used for training, they validate more problems than official cvc5 in ten of the 13 Divisions in 2026 and in eight in 2025, with geometric-mean gains of 7.8% and 6.8% across Divisions. On the complete official selections, which include training problems, the tuned floating-point counts exceed those of every individual competition participant in both years. Further studies show how configuration changes make existing algorithms effective by changing access to strategies, scheduling, and option compatibility, and how benchmark families trade off against one another. The agents' experiment traces contain hypothesis-based proposals in every tuning group, and 64.3% of the extracted hypotheses draw on prior measurements. These results show that agent-guided tuning can specialize a mature SMT solver and that accumulated experimental evidence informs sustained search.

title: Agent-Native by Design: A Programming Language for Agentic Applications
summary: Building agentic applications requires combining large language model (LLM) operations, workflow structure and application state, and model-guided routing. With SDKs and agent frameworks, developers connect these components through supporting code that prepares model inputs, propagates state, and dispatches model-selected steps. Workflow changes can require coordinated updates to this code, increasing development and testing effort. Splitting execution logic between application code and framework internals also limits compiler visibility into control flow and state dependencies, hindering automatic optimization. We introduce Agent-Native Programming, which unifies these three components with shared execution semantics. We realize this approach in Jac, a Python-superset language, through "by llm()" for typed model operations and tool use, Object-Spatial Programming for workflow structure and state, and "visit ... by llm()" for model-guided routing. The routing construct derives the model's choices from executable workflow steps and schedules the selected steps. This explicit connection between model decisions and program execution gives the compiler and runtime a common basis for dependency analysis and automatic optimization. Across five benchmarks and five baselines, Jac achieves a 1.8-8.7x reduction in AI-integration code relative to the OpenAI SDK, with competitive observed task quality and lower coding-agent development effort. Two case studies demonstrate speculative execution and service partitioning through configuration alone, using program analysis and runtime checks to preserve workflow behavior under stated conditions.

title: AgentFaultBench: State-Verified Evaluation of Tool-Fault Recovery
summary: Does recovery advice help an agent finish a task after a tool fails? AgentFaultBench evaluates LangGraph and CrewAI agents performing specified tasks in an isolated GitLab installation. We inject tool errors and check both the resulting files and issues and the required reads, verification and final response. The prompt supplies the expected issue and report text, so the task tests execution rather than content generation. In the primary comparison of 1,944 planned runs, advice changes success by -8.33, 0.00 and +1.06 percentage points relative to a neutral reminder; missing outcomes leave the latter two comparisons inconclusive. Later experiments test a revised recovery policy. GPT-4o mini improves, while Sol and Claude already complete the recoverable cases. In a separate 624-run study on six related tasks not previously used by that policy, the guided condition records 161 correct final states and one unknown outcome in 192 planned runs, versus 142/192 with neutral feedback. The gain lies between +9.90 and +10.42 pp when missing outcomes are included. Removing issue IDs gives 47/48 successes versus 46/48 with IDs; other execution information remains. A second checker agrees on 1,879 observed primary outcomes and 241 constructed test cases. No human validation was collected. The findings support testing advice against explicit recovery controls rather than assuming it helps.

title: An Efficient Training Paradigm for Image Restoration via Improved Fréchet Loss
summary: Diffusion-based image restoration achieves strong perceptual quality but typically relies on iterative sampling, leading to slow inference. Existing single-step methods often use diffusion distillation or adversarial training, complicating optimization. To simplify training, we propose FDIR, a framework for training single-pass generative restoration models through regression-style supervised optimization using directly computable objectives. To realize this paradigm, FDIR employs the Fréchet distance to match the feature distributions of restored and real images in frozen representation spaces, providing explicit distribution-level supervision. To better accommodate image restoration, we incorporate local patch features to capture fine-grained restoration discrepancies. Moreover, we introduce instance-adaptive statistics by combining the feature moments of each SR-HQ pair with synchronized historical statistics, allowing distribution matching to incorporate input-specific correspondence while retaining distribution-level context. FDIR optimizes only the LoRA parameters of the restoration backbone. Experiments demonstrate strong perceptual restoration quality and efficient training, suggesting a simpler paradigm for generative image restoration.

title: AnachroBench: Evaluating Historical Consistency in Large Vision-Language Models
summary: Existing Large Vision-Language Model benchmarks primarily evaluate visual understanding in general everyday scenarios, leaving historical consistency with a specified era and country largely underexplored. To address this gap, we propose AnachroBench, a controlled discriminative benchmark for evaluating historical consistency in visual scenes. It contains 1,600 image pairs from eight countries spanning the late 19th to the early 20th century, each pairing an original historical image with an anachronistic version containing a seamlessly inserted modern object. AnachroBench evaluates three aspects: Inserted Object Perception, which tests whether models detect the inserted modern object; Era-Country Consistency, which assesses whether the scene is consistent with the specified era and country; and Conditional Era-Country Consistency, which measures consistency judgments only when the inserted object is correctly perceived. A false consistency judgment occurs when a model perceives the modern object but still judges the scene as historically consistent. Overall, AnachroBench reveals a gap between inserted object perception and era-country consistency judgments, providing a targeted evaluation of this behavior.

title: Anchoring Motion, Refining Trajectories: Generalizable Continuous Neural Decoding
summary: Brain activity encodes motor information across multiple temporal scales, enabling continuous neural control beyond discrete action recognition. However, existing methods are typically tailored to specific subjects and tasks, with direct neural-to-kinematic mappings that can entangle subject-specific neural variability with task-dependent motion patterns, limiting generalization. To address these limitations, we introduce AMRT, a shared neural decoding framework for heterogeneous electrode configurations and movement paradigms. Motivated by cortical encoding of movement direction and speed, AMRT adopts a two-stage design that anchors local motion through velocity estimation and refines the resulting trajectories over longer horizons, encouraging reuse of local motion tendencies across subjects and tasks. Across three datasets, AMRT generalizes to unseen trials and subjects and demonstrates transfer potential across neural recordings and movement paradigms, highlighting the potential of shared neural representations and anchor-and-refine decoding for generalizable continuous neural control.

title: Anytime-Valid PAC-Bayes Certificates for Adaptive Test-Time Scaling
summary: Test-time scaling systems often choose how much to sample, which prompt to use, and which verifier or aggregation rule to trust after repeatedly inspecting a calibration set. Standard validation error bars are not valid after this adaptive selection. We model a test-time scaling recipe as a randomized predictor with a random cost and prove a time-uniform PAC-Bayes certificate that holds simultaneously over all calibration times, all posterior mixtures over recipes, and all data-dependent stopping rules. Thus the same event covers the recipe search that precedes deployment, not merely the fixed recipe finally reported. For a finite grid of budgets and verifiers, the penalty is the familiar $\log M/n$, which in the worst case no certificate valid after selection can avoid, while non-uniform priors and localized posterior mixtures can give sharper certificates for structured searches. We specialize the result to self-consistency and show a complementary margin law: plurality voting improves exponentially in the sample budget only on examples where the correct answer is the generator's unique mode; otherwise more compute can provably amplify errors. The same margin analysis yields an oracle water-filling law for compute allocation. A synthetic audit quantifies the optimism caused by adaptive budget selection, and a 192-example GSM8K audit using gpt-4.1-mini generations illustrates risk-cost reporting for a real inference pipeline. At scale, with two models on GSM8K and MATH-500, selected-best error bars fall below the out-of-split GSM8K risk in up to 22.5% of random splits at a nominal 5% while the certificate never does, and on the full GSM8K test split it tightens to 0.109 (held-out risk 0.039). The results give a lightweight, distribution-free way to report risk and compute claims for adaptive inference systems.

title: Architectural Principles for Parameter-Efficient Unitary Transformations in Coherent Optical Neural Networks
summary: Coherent optical neural networks based on interferometric architectures offer a promising route toward high-throughput, energy-efficient computation by exploiting the multiple degrees of freedom of light, including spatial, temporal, and spectral modes. However, practical implementations are constrained by the number of tunable parameters due to fabrication complexity, device footprint, and control overhead. In such parameter-constrained settings, achieving high expressive power remains a central challenge. We identify two key architectural requirements for maintaining high expressive power under these constraints: (i) statistical uniformity in the implemented transformations and (ii) strong mixing capability per parameter, which enables rapid and unbiased redistribution of information across modes. To realize these requirements, we develop a logarithmic-depth butterfly-topology architecture whose fundamental building block is a single phase-shifter--beam-splitter pair, in contrast to conventional rectangular mesh architectures based on Mach-Zehnder interferometers. Computational evaluations show that, particularly at restricted parameter counts, the proposed architecture achieves lower matrix-reconstruction errors and higher classification accuracies than conventional meshes in both feedforward and recurrent networks. We further quantify these design principles using graph-theoretic measures, expected squared moduli of transformation-matrix entries, and matrix-reconstruction error. The resulting framework provides a quantitative and physically interpretable basis for parameter-efficient optical neural networks.

title: AstroPIE-53: Towards Understanding Failure Modes of Human Pose Estimation in Space
summary: Reliable monitoring of astronauts is essential for safety, situational awareness, and autonomous assistance in space missions. While modern computer vision enables accurate human detection and pose estimation on Earth, its robustness in space environments remains largely unquantified due to limited data availability. We present AstroPIE-53, a pilot dataset of 53 annotated astronaut videos collected from publicly available mission footage. To respect copyright restrictions, we release video identifiers, reconstruction scripts, and dense annotations rather than raw videos. The dataset includes bounding boxes, challenge classes, and human-annotated pose failure tags. We benchmark state-of-the-art person detection and pose estimation models under realistic zero-shot deployment conditions and perform the first systematic failure analysis for astronaut monitoring. Our results reveal substantial performance degradation caused by occlusions, unusual body orientations, low contrast, and microgravity motion patterns.

title: Attention Sinks as Spectral Spikes: A Mechanism Analysis of Gated Attention
summary: Transformer attention exhibits attention sinks, where a small subset of source tokens absorbs disproportionate attention mass across layers. Recent work shows that post-SDPA output gating strongly reduces attention-sink behavior, while separate studies link attention sinks to gradient sinks and massive activations through backward training dynamics. Yet how the same gate affects forward sink structure, backward gradient concentration, and training-time representation signatures remains unclear. We address this gap by formulating attention sinks as sink-induced low-rank modes in token-space covariance, with directions aligned to high-mass attention columns. Under this view, post-SDPA gating acts as a mode-dependent contraction: it attenuates sink-induced spectral energy in the forward pass and locally reduces value-path gradients routed through sink columns in the backward pass. Empirically, random-matrix diagnostics show that gating reduces outlier mass, weakens sink-subspace alignment, and increases effective rank, while backward analyses show active-gate attenuation of first-token value gradients. Training-time diagnostics further show that gating suppresses the co-emergence of attention concentration, value-gradient amplification, and representation dominance.

title: Auditing a Moving Target: Evidence Anchoring and the Expiry of Fairness Audits of Provider-Served Language Models
summary: Organizations increasingly use large language models (LLMs) for decisions about people, such as hiring, investment and employee evaluation, and rely on them over long periods of time. Fairness audits of such systems, however, are conducted only once. We examine how the biases of LLMs change over time. In a venture screening setting, models from five providers decided whether and how much to invest in startups whose founders differed only in gender, origin and university. We repeated this audit three times over 13 months (248,400 API calls). Study 1 shows that the same model, called under the same identifier one year later, displayed a significantly different bias pattern. Study 2 shows that the successors of retired models carried the same bias as their predecessors, but in a significantly different size and form. Study 3 shows that the bias does not depend on the industry of the startup. A document analysis further shows that providers change and retire models at their discretion, with notice periods of zero to six months. Drawing on these findings, we develop a theory of evidence anchoring. We theorize that bias resides in the model class and persists, whereas audit evidence is anchored to a single model and expires when the provider decides. We derive policy advice for organizations and regulators, namely audits of model classes instead of single models, a version record for every model response, and re-audits triggered by model changes.

title: Balanced Twin Weight Factorization for Efficient MLLMs
summary: Weight Factorization (WF) methods aim to reduce a model's latency, memory, or both. These typically decompose a pretrained model into two or more factors that approximate the original model weights with fewer parameters and floating point operations (FLOPs). However, translating fewer FLOPs into reduced latency is challenging for WF methods in practice due to overhead introduced by replacing a single large weight matrix with multiple smaller ones. To address this, we propose Balanced Twin Weight Factorization (BTWF), which uses the unique structure of factorized models to simultaneously lower latency and increase learning capacity. Specifically, BTWF operates in the shared basis WF setting, where two or more layers are decomposed into a shared basis matrix and a layer-specific mixing matrix. If these shared layers have the same input (i.e., are twins), then we need only perform this shared forward pass once, reducing inference time. However, twin layers are often of varying sizes, and methods from prior work tend to favor the larger layer. In contrast, our approach boosts performance by combining Factor Component Balancing (FCB), which ensures every shared member is well represented in the selected factors, with Block Contribution Balancing (BCB), which considers downstream model effects. Further, we also show that an overparameterized BTWF, where some layer's factors result in higher FLOPs than the original during training, can boost task performance without additional resources at test time. Experiments on six models over nine benchmarks show BTWF obtains a 2-6% gain over the state-of-the-art without expensive finetuning (1-3.5% gain with it) at comparable computational costs.

title: Benchleaking Is Accelerating: Benchmark contamination has worsened sharply in the past month -- from post-training down to pre-training base models
summary: Benchmark contamination is not new, but recent model releases show it in a sharper form. We use the term benchleaking for the case in which a benchmark's own test examples enter training data, so that a score reflects recall rather than capability. This differs from benchmaxxing, which optimizes toward a benchmark without seeing its test set. We document two escalations over the past month. First, in post-training, the traces have become explicit: recent audits show an agent stating hidden test requirements it was never given in 23% of its attempts, where its predecessor did so in none, and continuing to follow them after the task is changed to contradict them (Schaeffer and Räuker, 2026; Lo and Lo, 2026). Second, the problem has reached pre-training. Using few-shot continuation on 20 benchmarks across four public base models, we find that some base models write out other test examples---complete questions, options, and answers---that appear nowhere in their input. For the recently released ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base, 96% of HumanEval problems leak with their reference implementations and 85% of OpenBookQA questions leak with their answers, against 9% and none for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base. To quantify what a reported score owes to such examples, we define an Anti-Hack score: the benchmark score recomputed with every leaked example marked wrong and the number of examples unchanged. Averaged over the suite, it costs DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base 1.5 points and Hy3-preview-Base 1.3, against 5.0 for MiMo-V2.5-Base and 16.6 for ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base. Open base models are the foundation of much downstream research, so benchleaking now affects more than leaderboard rankings. We call for decontamination reports and contamination-adjusted scores to become standard practice.

title: Benchmarking LLM Inference on Desktop-Scale NVIDIA Grace Blackwell Clusters
summary: Two NVIDIA DGX Spark GB10 systems connect directly over 200 GbE to serve larger language models and increase inference capacity, but the benefits depend on how they are deployed. We benchmark 17 open-weight checkpoints spanning dense and mixture-of-experts architectures, 8B to 235B parameters and four weight precisions on one and two RDMA-connected systems. Using vLLM, we compare tensor parallelism (TP=2), pipeline parallelism (PP=2) and a two-replica baseline at concurrency 1 to 64, with three independent launches per configuration. TP=2 delivers a median 1.59x peak-throughput gain over one Spark, versus 1.39x for PP=2 and has higher throughput in 93 of 96 matched comparisons with separated 95% Welch intervals. It reduces unloaded inter-token latency to 0.52x to 0.73x of one Spark, whereas PP=2 provides little reduction. TP=2 also achieves the highest goodput under a strict 100 ms inter-token latency objective wherever both strategies are supported and the objective is met. For models fitting on one Spark, TP=2 generally favors low-concurrency serving, while replication offers higher throughput at high concurrency. One Spark uses less GPU energy per output token at matched concurrency. Across three precision ladders, NVFP4 reduces unloaded latency more than adding a second Spark at BF16. NCCL microbenchmarks and comparisons with an earlier TCP campaign suggest that collective communication overhead contributes to the advantage of TP=2. These results provide deployment guidance for desktop-scale inference.

title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Linguistic Annotation
summary: Assessing large language models for linguistic annotation requires task-specific evaluation under documented conditions. We present dhAIBench, a Python benchmarking and annotation tool with a web interface for exploring and sharing results. It records prompts, configurations and predictions, enabling comparisons of annotation quality, confidence calibration, repeatability and estimated cost. We demonstrate the framework and the associated methodology through 293 runs of 48 models on nine linguistic annotation tasks spanning morphology, syntax, semantics, discourse-pragmatics, spelling normalization and learner-language correction. Models achieve high agreement with reference annotations on several tasks, including those on non-standardized, historical varieties as well as requiring contextual interpretation. The results support evaluating models against specific linguistic tasks, rather than relying on general rankings. To this end, we make the current and future benchmarks publicly available at dhaibench.silent3.ff.cuni.cz.

title: Beyond AUC: Do Mammography Risk Models Predict When Cancer Occurs?
summary: Longitudinal deep learning models for mammography-based breast cancer risk prediction output either per-year cumulative risks or a discrete distribution over the year of diagnosis, from which cumulative risks F1,...,F5 are derived. These models are evaluated almost exclusively with year-wise AUCs and the concordance index. We show that these metrics are largely insensitive to when cancer occurs: they can be high even for a model that carries no information about the year of diagnosis. We re-evaluate two recent longitudinal models (OA-BreaCR, LMV-Net) on CSAW-CC with a 5-year horizon using timing metrics computed on cancer cases only. Despite C-indices up to 0.75, neither orders cancer cases by time to diagnosis significantly better than chance (c_time 0.51 and 0.55, both 95% CIs covering 0.5). Weighted absolute timing error favours a constant "year 3" prediction over both models, so we use c_time as the primary timing metric. For Mirai's additive-hazard head, also used by LMV-Net, we analyse how per-year increments passed through a ReLU can collapse under severe class imbalance. We also propose a breast-level, two-stage model that separates whether from when. It matches LMV-Net in discrimination (C-index 0.745 vs. 0.746) but orders cancer cases better (c_time 0.58 vs. 0.51, paired 95% CI of the difference 0.01-0.13), on par with Mirai's published weights (0.57).

title: Beyond Family Labels: A Taxonomic Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Prior for Avian 3D Shape Recovery
summary: Recovering 3D pose and shape of birds from single images is bottlenecked by the long tail of avian diversity: out of ~10,000 species, only a few dozen have 3D-labeled training data, and in-the-wild test sets routinely contain species never seen at training. Generalizing across clades is therefore a central problem. The current state of the art, AniMer+, mitigates it with a family-level contrastive loss that conveys only a binary same-family indicator per pair and discards the continuous structure of the species tree. We propose a taxonomic Ornstein-Uhlenbeck prior on the shape code of the AVES parametric bird mesh model: a multivariate Gaussian whose covariance decays exponentially with Linnaean rank distance, with a learnable selection strength and noise scale. The prior generalizes family contrastive into a continuous, generative form, exposing the graded cross- and within-family similarity that a binary indicator cannot, and brings continuous comparative phylogenetics in as a biology-grounded inductive bias for the long tail. Our method improves over AniMer+ on both metrics of the unseen-species CowBird benchmark and on CtrlAVES3D, while remaining comparable on seen-species CUB. A permutation ablation isolates taxonomic structure from generic Gaussian smoothing, and a rank-granularity ablation identifies cross-order distinctions (the structure beyond a family-vs-not indicator) as the dominant source of the unseen-species gain.

title: Beyond Seeing: Fine-Grained Preference Validation and Severity-Aware Alignment for Mitigating Visual Hallucinations in Vision-Language Models
summary: Large vision-language models can produce fluent responses containing objects, attributes, or relations unsupported by the image. We study an implemented alignment pipeline that normalizes released fine-grained hallucination supervision, validates chosen-rejected preference pairs with vision-language judges, repairs rejected chosen responses, and trains LLaVA adapters with standard or severity-aware direct preference optimization. The study uses 16,143 normalized feedback records and 8,386 released preference pairs, comparing direct training with zero-shot and two-shot judged severity-margin variants. The zero-shot variant reduces Object HalBench CHAIRs from 53.00 to 36.00 and CHAIRi from 15.72 to 10.41. Across aligned models, AMBER-Hal decreases from 35.90 to 25.10-26.90, accompanied by reduced visual coverage. In contrast, the base model retains the highest valid POPE adversarial F1, 84.18 versus 83.87-83.91 after alignment. These results support benchmark-dependent reductions in generative hallucination rather than uniform superiority of severity-aware alignment. We distinguish implemented pipeline components from the preference paths used in the reported experiments and discuss the limits of attributing gains to judging, repair, or the training objective individually.

title: Beyond Token Stacking: Multi-scale Visual Modulation and Adaptive Fused-feature Calibration for MLLMs
summary: Current Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have advanced rapidly and follow two main paradigms: one involves concatenating visual and textual tokens for input into Large Language Model (LLM), while the other injects visual knowledge into Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) of the LLM. However, the former introduces a large number of redundant visual tokens, substantially increasing computational overhead. The latter reduces sequence length but removes images from the input stage entirely, which may hinder the activation of image-related knowledge. Moreover, naively injecting visual knowledge into the FFNs could induce activation distribution shifts due to cross-modal semantic discrepancies. To address these challenges, we develop Beyond Token Stacking (BTS), a novel visual enhancement framework for MLLMs. Specifically, we propose a Multi-scale Visual Modulation (MVM) mechanism that injects multi-scale visual information at the input stage via modulation without increasing the token sequence length. Furthermore, we develop an Adaptive Fused-feature Calibration (AFC) module that performs per-channel affine calibration to decouple visual injection from distribution alignment in the FFN layers, improving multimodal fusion stability while preserving language priors. Experiments show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance.

title: BiGSyn: A Bi-Level Heterogeneous Graph Contrastive Learning Framework for Interpretable Drug Synergy Prediction
summary: Drug combination therapy has become a mainstream of modern medicine, with the potential to enhance efficacy, reduce toxicity, and overcome drug resistance. However, identifying synergistic drug combinations remains challenging, as it requires modeling complex interactions across multiple biological scales---from atom-level molecular structures to entity-level relations in biological networks. Existing approaches typically model these levels in isolation, overlooking complementary signals and long-range dependencies. To address these limitations, we propose BiGSyn, a Bi-level heterogeneous Graph contrastive learning framework for drug Synergy prediction. Specifically, BiGSyn leverages heterogeneous graph transformers to extract high-order dependencies from molecular graphs and biological networks, and introduces a bi-level contrastive learning objective to bridge the cross-level semantic gap. Extensive experiments on two benchmark datasets show that BiGSyn consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Moreover, its attention mechanism highlights key molecular substructures and biological interactions driving synergy, providing interpretable insights.

title: BlockAlign: Preference Optimization for Trajectory-Distilled Video Generation
summary: Directly aligning trajectory-distilled video generators slashes rollout costs and optimizes the deployed few-step model without teacher fine-tuning or re-distillation. However, conventional flow-matching preference objectives assume single-head local velocity supervision, mismatching the finite-interval, block-average transition interface of trajectory-distilled generators such as Parallel Decoding Distillation (PDD) and Parametric Trajectory Distillation (PTD). Naively supervising only the primary initial-subinterval velocity sub-head rather than the fused block-average velocity at block starts (DirectAlign) induces a severe training--inference mismatch that degrades quality below the unaligned baseline. We introduce BlockAlign, an interface-consistent preference optimization framework that constructs states at valid block boundaries, queries the fused block-level velocity predictor, and supervises span-normalized transition residuals-seamlessly supporting DPO-, NFT-, and rollout-style objectives while preserving the native few-step sampler. We further build a unified post-training pipeline integrating offline pairs, reward-free semi-online continuations, and online rollouts with hierarchical preference selection and objective-aware block scheduling. Experiments on multi-reference video generation across MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA and an in-house model RefVid-V4 show that BlockAlign consistently outperforms unaligned distilled models and DirectAlign in structural plausibility, reference consistency, and visual quality. Notably, our approach unlocks PDD's 5x few-step rollout speedup for 3x faster end-to-end online training, achieving statistically significant human preference gains over PDD baselines (54.0% vs. 33.3% wins/losses, or 61.8% non-tie win rate on RefVid-V4; 51.3% vs. 34.7%, or 59.7% non-tie win rate on MiniMax-H3) and up to an 82.7% win rate against DirectAlign.

title: Body of Evidence: Triangulating 3D Human Pose with Geometry-Conditioned Depth
summary: Even in multi-camera setups, occlusions can leave individual body joints with only a single usable 2D observation. Such an observation defines a viewing ray but leaves the joint's depth undetermined. We introduce Body of Evidence (BoE), a multi-view 3D human pose estimator that predicts per-camera joint depths alongside 2D joint locations. To reduce monocular depth ambiguity, we propose geometry-conditioned depth prediction, which combines image features with previously reconstructed 3D body geometry as contextual depth cues. We further introduce learnable depth-aware triangulation (LDAT), which augments differentiable algebraic triangulation with predicted depth constraints, enabling reconstruction even from a single contributing camera while preserving the benefits of geometric triangulation when multiple views are available. The reconstructed 3D poses subsequently guide depth prediction in the next iteration, allowing depth estimates and 3D geometry to progressively refine each other. Experiments on CMU Panoptic demonstrate state-of-the-art in-domain performance and superior average performance across evaluated camera subsets and unseen camera arrangements. BoE is particularly effective under sparse camera coverage, outperforming the previous state of the art by 10.6 AP25 points in the challenging three-camera setting.

title: Bookkeeping Is Not Judgement: EJBench, an Engineering Judgement Benchmark Built from a Conjugate Heat Transfer Design Campaign
summary: We introduce EJBench, a benchmark of engineering judgement: whether a model can predict how a design behaves at new conditions from a few earlier results, and decide on it. Unlike engineering benchmarks that test whether an agent can operate simulation or CAD software, EJBench is software-agnostic and asks what an engineer would conclude without running a simulation. Its tasks come from a conjugate heat transfer design campaign for battery cold plates, in three families: matching unlabelled test results to their operating points, choosing which stored runs to reveal before signing off a design, and ranking new duties by peak cell temperature. Every answer is taken from a converged simulation, not from an LLM judge. The best of ten frontier models, GPT-6 Astra, scores 0.71, and models state almost the same confidence on tasks they get wrong as on tasks they get right. We also post-train Qwen3.5-9B with LoRA and reinforcement learning, rewarded by the share of answer criteria the simulation results confirm; on the held-out test split its score rises from 0.071 to 0.106. We release the train, validation and test splits, the evaluation harness and the leaderboard.

title: Breaking feature collapse in self-supervised time series encoders
summary: General-purpose time series encoders promise a single backbone that generalises across tasks and domains; however, they currently do not scale. We trace this down to a critical point of failure: under the predominant masked data modelling supervision, the encoder's output tokens partially collapse. This is the natural consequence of supervising encoders only in the input space, which leaves no constraint against redundant token dimensions in the feature space. We introduce OTISv2, which suppresses the collapse by complementing the reconstruction objective in input space with two objectives in the feature space: a self-distillation loss against an exponential-moving-average teacher, and a KoLeo regulariser. Under matched training, the resulting encoder reduces the cosine similarity and lifts the effective rank of its output tokens relative to its predecessor, and it scales monotonically from 7.1 M to 116 M parameters where its predecessor declines. It matches or surpasses existing general-purpose time series encoders across 143 uni- and multi-variate datasets. To foster further research, we release our code and pre-trained weights.

title: CAE-Bench: Benchmarking AI Agents for Reusable CAE Solver Development
summary: We developed CAE-Bench, a benchmark to evaluate AI agents on Computer-Aided Engineering (CAE) solver development. A CAE solver is more than a PDE solver; it must be able to generalize across various inputs, such as different boundary conditions, geometries, and material properties. CAE-Bench evaluates the generalizability of AI-developed CAE solvers by providing the same task, such as a heat transfer problem, multiple cases, with each case specifying an input. The AI agent develops a solver for a fixed task using only a few public cases, and the resulting solver is then tested on held-out cases, i.e., cases it has never seen before. We evaluate 12 models across a range of reasoning settings on 80 computational tasks. Our experiments show that even if a solver developed by an AI agent performs well on the public cases, it may even get 0 score on held-out cases. For tasks such as fluid dynamics problems, even the solver developed by GPT-6 Astra performs poorly on held-out cases. A data format and an SDK for task registration are provided, so the researcher can use the benchmark on their own infrastructure. We hope that CAE-Bench will help the community to develop AI agents that can develop reusable CAE solvers that generalize to various inputs.

title: CLIFT: Contrastive LiDAR Instance Features for 3D Pedestrian Tracking
summary: A social robot has to keep track of the people around it over time to plan its motion, a task handled by 3D multi-object tracking. For the LiDAR modality, trackers usually sit on top of a detector and link its detections across frames with a separate motion model or re-identification network. We instead show how a 3D LiDAR detector itself can be turned into a tracker by adding an instance-level contrastive objective on its intermediate voxel features. Each embedding is read from the voxels inside a detected box, and boxes are matched across frames by cosine similarity and the Hungarian algorithm, without a motion model. The detector backbone is fine-tuned together with this objective, which learns identity-aware features while leaving detection accuracy essen- tially intact. Because the method uses only the voxel features that Li- DAR detectors already produce, it is backbone-agnostic. On the JRDB 3D tracking leaderboard our LiDAR-only tracker ranks first on HOTA (38.58) and IDF1 (37.99), 13.04 and 9.30 points above the next pub- lished method, and second on MOTA and OSPA. Code is available at https://hermak56.github.io/CLIFT/.

title: CONGA: Compiling Gaussian Fiber Geometry for Structured Bayesian Inference
summary:
In structured Bayesian models, a large latent block is often Gaussian conditional on a smaller set of parameters, yet generic inference methods relearn this geometry during warmup. We study how this structure can be used to construct transports for posterior inference. The conditional mean and precision determine exact affine maps, including symmetric Brenier and triangular Knothe-Rosenblatt maps, that separate a standard normal block from the remaining non-Gaussian core. KL and relative Fisher objectives then reduce to objectives on this core. We introduce CONGA, a compiler that identifies candidate Gaussian blocks and selects a temporal, spectral, or sparse implementation according to their structure and computational cost. Marginalization requires an identity established from the model; numerical evidence alone permits only a target-preserving change of variables, and a failed check leaves the model unchanged. On the Stock-Watson inflation model, CONGA improves minimum ESS per second by 12.5x for NUTS. It also restores convergence where the raw target fails: for WALNUTS on the same model, and for NUTS on a 6760-dimensional electricity load model reduced to 34 core coordinates. Experiments on graph-indexed fields show how coloring and fill affect the choice of map, including cases where retaining the original target is preferable.
  Code at https://github.com/vicgalle/conga

title: Calibrate Once, Grow the Vocabulary: Candidate-Independent Scores for Conformal Risk Control in Open-Vocabulary Segmentation
summary: Open-vocabulary segmenters accept class names at inference. Conformal risk control can bound how often their prediction sets miss the true label, but we show that this bound breaks when names are added after calibration. On ADE20K, a threshold calibrated for 10% risk at 150 names reaches up to 15.4% risk at 845 names in released CAT-Seg models. The risk exceeds the target on every calibration split, yet the prediction sets grow far less than the target requires. In SED they instead grow larger than needed. The cause is that pruning, cross-label attention and vocabulary normalisation make each label's score depend on the other requested labels. Scores can move either way, so a threshold recalibrated at a larger vocabulary need not hold at smaller ones. We remove this dependence without training by scoring each label against a fixed reference bank of names. A label's score then stays the same when names are added, so one calibration keeps its guarantee as the vocabulary grows. The guarantee holds whatever names are added, even ones chosen per image after seeing it. On three benchmarks and five segmenters, the converted models meet the target at every vocabulary size we evaluate. For CAT-Seg and SED at alpha=10%, they use at most one more label per pixel than the released models recalibrated at the grown vocabulary. Treating names instead of images as calibration samples also bounds the miss rate of added names. If the annotated names are a random sample of the names in the calibration images, an added name's expected miss rate on those images is at most the target. For harder added names, the excess is at most their gap in mean miss rate. Applied to Grounding DINO, which splits large vocabularies into chunks, the conversion also makes inference about six times faster.

title: Calibrated Functional Prediction from Overlapping Nonlinear Observations
summary: We study prediction of nonlinear audit functionals from scalar observations of a shared hidden table state. For Schur-rational operators, local Gaussian projections yield a common sparse kernel for overlapping tasks, repeated row identities, and cross-row dependence. Shared-state residual samples extend this kernel through a positive-semidefinite feature representation. Positive matrix integration and sample-value enclosures connect the original inputs to the actual saved hybrid prediction. A sorted calibration-role perturbation bound then certifies its complete finite-pool pinball risk. Independent complete-loss selection chooses the ridge, score scale, and residual weight, while task-rank calibration supplies an upper endpoint. Evaluation uses twenty new reference contexts per dataset at two task sizes, giving 400 conditions across ten benchmark populations. The mean dataset complete-loss ratios are 0.9977 to the degree-two kernel, 0.9961 to matched complete-MC shrinkage, and 0.9911 to the retrospective minimum over 174 public configurations. The last ratio has a paired reference-bootstrap interval of [0.9898,0.9927]. On 40 profiles at coefficient tolerance $10^{-7}$, Gamma quadrature has a geometric mean cold-time ratio of .0646 to strengthened Arb/Petras integration.

title: Calpha: Toward Native Biomolecular Intelligence in a General-Purpose Language Model
summary: Biomolecular foundation models predict the structures of proteins and their complexes accurately, and large language models (LLMs) reason in natural language, but the two remain separate: the abilities of the former are not part of a general-purpose LLM, and the reasoning of the latter does not enter a structure prediction. Calpha aims at one general model that folds proteins and complexes, understands protein sequence and structure, and lets its language reasoning influence the structures it predicts. This report covers the first step, in which an LLM outputs single-chain protein structures. Qwen3.5-9B reads a sequence enriched with ESM2 residue features. It can respond in text or emit a token that invokes a pretrained SimpleFold structure head, which receives information about the protein only through Qwen's residue states. Under a fixed folding request, the head achieves mean TM-scores of 0.808 on the FoldBench-334 development set, 0.635 on CASP16 domains and 0.900 on a CAMEO-style PDB set. We compare these predictions with a baseline in which ESM2-3B encodes the sequence and a fine-tuned SimpleFold-3B head predicts the coordinates. The two systems also differ in trainable weights, training duration and crop length. For chains of 100--299 residues, all three paired confidence intervals include zero. At 300--600 residues, the mean differences are -0.044, -0.160 and -0.025, respectively. In a separate test, four English request types triggered folding on every evaluated example. Protein training reduced accuracy on a 350-item MMLU-Pro subset from 77.4% to 70.3%. An LLM can therefore output single-chain structures from its own states, with lower long-chain scores in the current comparisons and reduced accuracy on the evaluated MMLU-Pro subset. Complex prediction, structure understanding and the effect of language reasoning on the predicted coordinates remain future work.

title: Can AI Mature a Model's Geometry? Training-Free Weight Baking in LLMs
summary: Can an AI make a trained language model more mature, in the sense of a better organized latent space, by looking only at the geometry of that space? An analyst model reads a fixed-size digest of topological descriptors of the layers of a frozen target and proposes a transformation, which closed-form ridge regression writes into the feed-forward weights without gradient training. Using lightweight models, 126 runs show that category purity rose on unseen words and sentences, benchmark accuracy stayed within sampling error, and the analyst matched a category-aware heuristic with gentler edits. In a five-model round robin approach, 16 pairs raised purity and four left the target unchanged. The results provide a baseline for future work on LLM-guided, training-free model editing without using raw weights.

title: Can Image Generators Hold a Scene Together When Space Is Broken Apart?
summary: Image generators are good at drawing scenes in which things that belong together appear next to each other. In almost every image they generate, and in almost every benchmark used to evaluate these images, "belonging to the same whole" and "adjacent to each other" go together. Therefore, we cannot know whether the model truly grasps the scene as a whole, or simply makes each part connect with its adjacent parts. We propose GJBench to disentangle the two. It requires the model to draw a scene as a scattered jigsaw puzzle: an image is cut into interlocking pieces, then moved apart and rotated. Thus, the spatial plausibility of the scene exists only in how these pieces collectively point to a whole. The model may have a reference image, a target layout, both, or neither. We separately evaluate three requirements: whether the scene is broken down into a specified number of separate pieces, whether the pieces interlock, and whether the pieces can reconstruct the reference scene. While every open and closed model we evaluated could draw these scenes well as a whole, none could keep them together as scattered puzzle pieces, and the three requirements categorized failures into different patterns. The models draw separate pieces but miscount them in different ways, and unless their outlines are provided, the pieces rarely interlock, and their content does not reconstruct the reference image. We also found that the target layout helps the puzzle pieces fit together, while the reference image improves neither their count nor their fit. These findings show that keeping a scene continuous across space that the canvas no longer shows remains an open problem for image generators.

title: Canonical activation patterns and ReLU pattern varieties
summary: A ReLU pattern variety records the polynomial relations among the coefficients of the affine maps associated with a prescribed set of activation patterns of a ReLU network. We study how the combinatorics of the canonical set of activation patterns of an unbiased ReLU network is reflected in the geometry of its pattern variety. In particular, we introduce the notion of pattern stability and characterize pattern stability and combinatorial stability for shallow networks. When the associated wall graph is connected and contains an edge of every neuron label, we resolve a problem of Alexandr and Montúfar by determining the defining ideal of the associated pattern variety explicitly. We establish a hierarchy of progressively weaker equivalence relations relating labeled combinatorial equivalence, equality and permutation equivalence of canonical pattern sets, and equivalences of the associated varieties. Finally, we relate functional dimension to the differential of the pattern map and show that it is bounded above by the dimension of the canonical pattern variety at every depth. For nondegenerate shallow networks, we give an exact formula for the functional dimension; for every shallow architecture, it equals the dimension of the canonical pattern variety on an open dense set of full Lebesgue measure.

title: Cap-Aware Boosting for Green Day-Ahead Electricity Price Forecasting
summary: Accurate forecasting of Green Day-Ahead Market (GDAM) electricity prices is essential for market participants in the Indian power sector. We present a LightGBM-based forecasting framework for Indian Energy Exchange GDAM prices, which clear in 96 fifteen-minute intervals per day. The proposed system explicitly models price-cap behavior by separating capped-price events from normal market conditions. A classification head estimates the probability of the regulatory price cap (Rs 10,000/MWh), while a regression head predicts uncapped prices in logarithmic space. Final forecasts are obtained through probabilistic blending of these components and are accompanied by nine quantile forecasts for uncertainty estimation. Evaluated on 257 trading days between 1 January and 14 September 2026, the model achieves a mean absolute error (MAE) of 397.9 Rs/MWh and a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 9.57%, substantially outperforming a Chronos-2 baseline (583.3 MAE) and a persistence baseline using the previous day's profile (589.1 MAE). We further introduce leak-safe variants that incorporate real-time market signals, unmatched sell volumes, and solar generation proxies. In a recent out-of-sample evaluation, the quantile-clock variant achieved the best short-term performance with an MAE of 789 Rs/MWh during 25-28 October, while the enhanced capped-price model achieved an MAE of 716 Rs/MWh across 21 evaluation days through 16 November. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of regime-aware probabilistic forecasting for high-volatility electricity markets.

title: Certified, Not Explained: Exact Token Erasure in Gated Vision State Space Models
summary: Vision models built on Mamba are often explained through their selective step size Delta, on the assumption that a token the scan does not admit cannot influence the prediction. We test that in a concept bottleneck model for lung-nodule malignancy built on a single gated, bidirectional selective state-space block. The answer becomes an interpretability framework: a guarantee, a procedure that checks it, and a pre-registered audit of what it explains. For a fixed gate pattern, masking the input of the causal convolution of the block and giving closed tokens zero weight at readout makes the concept and task logits exactly invariant to the closed tokens. Gating Delta is neither necessary nor sufficient. On LIDC-IDRI, a path-by-path knockout over 15 cross-validated models agrees with this in every run: the largest logit change is exactly 0 whenever the conditions hold and between 4.1 and 6.7 when they do not. The gated model reaches a pooled out-of-fold AUROC of 0.8425 +/- 0.0085, level with an ungated Mamba bottleneck (0.8428). The guarantee belongs to the masked model, not to the gate as an explanation. Post-hoc rankers, which inherit the guarantee on this model, order tokens better than the gate. Gate maps from a model trained on permuted labels are as close to the real maps as two real-label seeds are to each other. Under retraining, the tokens of the gate carry more task information than random tokens and, on shifted crops, more than central ones, but no more than the tokens chosen by hidden attention. We therefore read the gate as a certified support set produced by mask supervision. Splitting the Oracle Impurity Score into own-concept and cross-concept parts reveals differences the aggregate score misses. Partitioning the readout reduced leakage slightly under an earlier recipe, and the final model sits at, rather than below, the level implied by correlations among the true concepts.

title: CiGS: Conduction in Gaussian Splats for Interior Temperature Field from Thermal Images
summary: We present a method for inferring the interior temperature distribution of a solid object from registered multi-view visible-spectrum and thermal images, even when the thermal views cover only part of its surface. We formulate steady-state heat conduction as a Laplace boundary value problem and solve it with a direct boundary integral equation discretized over a point cloud: a Gaussian reconstruction of the visible-spectrum images supplies the boundary geometry, and the thermal images supply the boundary data. We do not build surface or volume meshes at any stage in our method. Instead, we sample collocation points from rendered depth without the pixels at depth discontinuities, and use a density subtraction that keeps the interior evaluation accurate up to the surface. The whole chain is differentiable, and we use it to recover the pose and depth of heating pipes, insulation defects, and the shape of cracks from thermal images. We validate our method through experiments on boundary value problems with Dirichlet-only and mixed Dirichlet and Robin boundaries, using synthetic and real captured data on scenes with challenging topology. These experiments show that our method matches analytical solutions and has better accuracy than FEM solvers.

title: CivilBench: Benchmarking Vision-Language Models for Multimodal Information Integration in Civil Engineering
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs), is increasingly applied in civil and structural engineering for disaster assessment, structural analysis, and engineering decision support. However, the extent to which current VLMs possess the reasoning capabilities required for reliable engineering judgments remains unclear. In this work, we introduce CivilBench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating VLMs in civil engineering and disaster-related scenarios. CivilBench covers three major task families: Sequential Reasoning, Image-based Structural Understanding, and Open-world Understanding, encompassing numerical reasoning, structural damage assessment, risk inference, causal analysis, and repair planning. The benchmark is constructed through a systematic pipeline of domain-specific data collection, engineering-oriented captioning, expert annotation, question design, and quality verification. Evaluation of representative state-of-the-art VLMs reveals substantial limitations in domain-specific reasoning, with Sequential Reasoning emerging as a major bottleneck, particularly when models must infer numerical relationships from sparse structured observations. Further experiments show that numerical priors and external knowledge can alleviate these limitations, although their effectiveness depends on the model's ability to reliably interpret and use the available evidence. CivilBench provides a capability-oriented testbed for identifying reasoning limitations and evaluating progress toward reliable AI-assisted engineering decision-making. The benchmark will be publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/traceuryuan/CivilBench.

title: Classical structural priors improve neural molecular representations in molecule language models
summary: Classical molecular similarity is central to chemical information systems, yet molecule-language models trained on paired structure-text data do not necessarily organize molecular embeddings according to graded structural relationships. Here we introduce Structure-Aware Guided Alignment (SAGA), a training-only regularizer that uses Centered Kernel Alignment to align neural molecular representations with fingerprint-based Tanimoto similarity, without adding parameters or requiring fingerprints at inference. In MolCA and Atomas, SAGA improves molecule-text retrieval, shifts non-exact retrieval toward closer structural analogues, and increases average scaffold-split property-prediction performance, while molecular description and text-to-molecule generation are improved or preserved in single-run ablations. These results show that established chemoinformatics priors can make molecule-language representations more chemically faithful while retaining their multimodal utility.

title: Comfort as a Constraint or as a Cost in Reinforcement Learning and Model Predictive Building Control
summary: A building controller that keeps a zone within comfort bounds at minimum energy can treat the bounds as a soft constraint, by adding the weighted violation to its cost, or as a hard constraint. We analyze the effect of the hard and the soft formulation of the same problem and isolate the effect of the formulation from the effect of the algorithm. To this end, we measure the difference in energy use between the two formulations on the BOPTEST bestest_hydronic_heat_pump case, in model predictive control (MPC) and in reinforcement learning (RL). The soft formulations are a weighted MPC and weighted SAC and DDPG learners, each at twelve weights. The hard formulations are an MPC with an exact penalty and the Lagrangian learners SAC-Lagrangian and primal-dual DDPG. We find that the hard formulations use more energy than the soft formulations at the largest weight, but violate the comfort bounds less. For a large weight, the soft formulation approaches the behavior of the hard formulation. The frontiers of the energy-comfort trade-off of the three weighted controllers lie close to each other, and the weight selects an operating point on this frontier. Under the soft formulation, the three algorithms reach very similar operating points, although at somewhat different weights. For this HVAC problem, the formulation and the weight thus affect the energy use more than the choice of algorithm.

title: Comments on "Deep Fréchet Regression"
summary: We discuss the Journal of the American Statistical Association (JASA) discussion paper "Deep Fréchet Regression" and explore an alternative perspective based on conditional flow matching. We propose learning covariate-dependent transport directly within the response space, avoiding separate manifold learning and reverse mapping. This perspective offers a potentially more flexible framework for incorporating geometric structure and modeling full conditional distributions.

title: Compressed Simulation-Based Inference: Neural Posterior Estimation for Massive Data via Low-Dimensional Sketches
summary: Neural posterior estimation (NPE) is a popular Bayesian simulation-based inference (SBI) approach that uses neural networks trained on simulated data--parameter pairs to approximate the posterior given a user-chosen prior. For high-dimensional observations, NPE methods typically approximate the conditional density of the parameter given a user-chosen or learned summary statistic, rather than the entire dataset, due to the curse of dimensionality. However, both approaches face challenges: hand-crafting good summaries for complex models requires considerable effort from scientists, while learning them from massive datasets can be prohibitively computationally expensive. To address these challenges, we propose approximating the conditional density of a parameter given low-dimensional sketches of the data. We show that, for a model with a $p$-dimensional parameter, only $2p+1$ random sketches are needed for posterior consistency. We compare with state-of-the-art embedding networks for NPE, and we find that our method \emph{matches} the best embedding network's performance while \emph{increasing computational efficiency}.

title: Conditional Diffusion Models for Amortized Bayesian System Identification
summary: Generative diffusion models rapidly solve Bayesian inverse problems, such as image restoration and inpainting, with a single trained model and without retraining for each new observation or task. Bayesian system identification, which typically involves inferring the hidden states and parameters of a dynamical system from measurements, poses a closely related inverse problem. Yet it is often addressed with computationally heavy Monte Carlo methods that must be rerun for every new measurement record. Moreover, these methods are restricted to a single inference task, and their cost grows with the state dimension and the record length. To alleviate these restrictions, we interpret Bayesian system identification in hiddem Markov models (HMMs) as a general Bayesian inverse problem, taking advantage of conditional diffusion models. Specifically, a transformer-based diffusion model is trained once on short segments of simulated trajectories to approximate the joint posterior of states and parameters. Through an attention mask induced by the Markov property and a relative time encoding, it can then be deployed on any new measurement record of custom length. At inference time, the same model can flexibly and rapidly be conditioned for joint state and parameter inference, state smoothing, parameter inference, or reconstructing missing measurements, without retraining. We demonstrate these capabilities on four benchmark systems and examine how the length of the training segments affects state and parameter inference. On records five times longer than the training segments, the model maintains its state accuracy, whereas comparison methods either show a more than tenfold error increase or require ten times as much sampling time.

title: Conflict-Aware Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation in Aligned Action Spaces for Cross-Game Generalization
summary: Zero-shot cross-game generalization aims to consolidate accessible source-game experts into a single vision-language model (VLM) that controls unseen games from raw pixels without target-game parameter updates. While multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) mitigates offline exposure bias and single-game reinforcement learning (RL) overfitting, scaling it to autoregressive VLMs faces two bottlenecks. First, token-to-action misalignment from subword length bias distorts discrete action probabilities and uncertainty margins. Second, multi-teacher policy conflict arises as source teachers under incompatible dynamics issue contradictory closed-loop corrections, causing negative transfer. We propose CAMOPD (Conflict-Aware Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation), a post-training framework that resolves multi-teacher policy conflict within an aligned semantic action space. CAMOPD first uses complete-action alignment to normalize command completion likelihoods over each game's legal action set, forming a calibrated categorical policy that provides reliable uncertainty margins for selective on-policy retention and visual specialist probes that can be evaluated across source games. To resolve policy conflict without target-game data, conflict-aware multi-teacher consolidation cross-evaluates these specialists across source games to capture both visual identifiability and inter-teacher compatibility, upweighting compatible teachers while suppressing conflicting corrections. On GameWorld's temporal and directional transfer suites with Qwen3.5-4B, CAMOPD achieves 26/30 (86.7%) and 24/30 (80.0%) Task-1 zero-shot success on unseen GeoDash and Doodle Jump, outperforming prompting, weight-merging, and multi-task baselines.

title: Conformal Expert Pools: Training-Free Probabilistic Time-Series Forecasting Beyond Seasonality
summary: Conformal Seasonal Pools (CSP) showed that a forecaster with no training at all, built only from past values at the same point in the season and from past forecast errors, significantly outperformed DeepNPTS, Amazon's learned non-parametric forecaster. We propose Conformal Expert Pools (CEP), a training-free successor. CEP replaces the single seasonal-naive forecast by a pool of simple forecasters, builds its predictive distribution from their past forecast errors, and adapts both the pool and the errors to the series being forecast. No model is trained and no parameter is learned across series. On the CSP benchmark of 232 datasets and 24,502 forecast windows, CEP is better than CSP on 78% of datasets by CRPS, on 84% by MSIS and on 83% by Winkler score; on a typical dataset its CRPS is 14% lower and its MSIS 23% lower (both p < 1e-22, paired Wilcoxon test), and coverage of 95% intervals rises from 90.1% to 92.2%. CEP has a lower CRPS than DeepNPTS on 88% of datasets, than NPTS on 89% and than SeasonalNPTS on 83%. The improvement persists on dataset families outside the development set and on 36 additional fev-bench files. We also test the published claims that Laplace, an online ensemble forecaster, "beats (almost) everything" and "beats" CSP. On 228 datasets at multi-step horizons the claims do not hold: CSP outperforms Laplace on 60% of datasets by CRPS and on 64% by interval score, and Laplace ranks sixth of seven methods, with the widest intervals of all (69% wider than CEP's). Its point forecast is biased low and on 54% of datasets is less accurate than seasonal naive, and from a cold start it takes about 7,700 times longer than CSP. CEP is better than Laplace on 82% of datasets by CRPS and on 80% by MSIS, with intervals about 40% narrower, and runs 271 times faster.

title: Conic Structure of the Cross-Entropy Loss at the Final Layer and Its Absence in Rectifier Backbones
summary: Slices of the loss along lines and planes in parameter space are widely used to visualize deep networks. They often show a single basin with nearly straight walls, which raises the question of whether such a loss is a cone rounded at its apex, or a lower envelope of several cones that meet along creases. We answer this question for softmax cross-entropy at two levels of a classifier. Over the weights of an affine final layer, the loss equals a polyhedral cone plus an offset that decreases monotonically and exponentially along every ray, towards a limit in closed form. The distance at which the asymptotic wall reaches the height of the starting point, which we call the core radius, equals the mean surprisal of the classes that the direction favours, divided by the slope of the wall. Over the parameters of a rectifier backbone, the loss along a line has a kink wherever the activation pattern of a sample changes. Using the dimension theory of semialgebraic sets, we show that, along almost every line, the samples that switch at one point share an irreducible factor of their pre-activation polynomials. Under a coprimality condition, each kink therefore carries the share of one sample among $n$, so creases comparable to the slope do not form. Measurements on ResNet-18 and ResNet-56 trained on CIFAR-10 illustrate both results, with a test that bounds the size of any crease that sampled loss values can hide.

title: Contrastive Activation-Guided Zeroth-Order Preference Optimisation for Memory-Efficient LLM Alignment
summary: Direct Preference Optimisation (DPO) simplifies reinforcement learning from human feedback, but still relies on traditional backpropagation and its associated activation-memory cost. Zeroth-order (ZO) optimisation avoids backpropagation, yet isotropic perturbations can produce noisy updates for preference objectives defined by differences between chosen and rejected responses. We introduce Contrastive Activation-guided Zeroth-Order Direct Preference Optimisation (CA-ZODPO), which constructs a low-rank search subspace from the activation discrepancy between the chosen and rejected responses in each preference pair. Perturbations are restricted to this subspace, while momentum is maintained in low-rank coordinates to preserve the memory advantages of ZO training. On Qwen2.5-1.5B with Anthropic HH-RLHF, CA-ZODPO outperforms common ZO baselines and remains competitive with first-order DPO in pairwise preference evaluation. It also reduces peak GPU memory by about 59\% at a sequence length of 2048 while retaining the sequence-length scaling behaviour of zeroth-order training.

title: Conversing with a Conversational Agent: A Real Conversation, Not a Simulated One
summary: The claim that interactions with artificial conversational agents merely simulate human conversation rests on a philosophical distinction between reproducing the observable features of an activity and actually performing it. Although this distinction is appropriate for certain physical phenomena, its application to linguistic and symbolic activities is far less straightforward. This article argues that conversations with large language model (LLM)-based agents are genuine conversational activities rather than mere simulations, without thereby attributing consciousness, subjective understanding, or human intentionality to artificial systems. Drawing on the distinction between subjective and objective simulation, the article first examines the limitations of defining conversation exclusively through the intrinsic properties of its participants.
