Controlled injections and retrospective Cartesian $k$-space undersampling further support fine-detail localization and degradation robustness. The discarded POD tail is only $3.8\%$ of the retained fine-error magnitude, and Med-PODiff improves downstream segmentation consistency while requiring substantially less inference time than pixel-space diffusion.

title: Is 4 Bits Enough for EEG Sleep Staging? A Subject-Level Benchmark of MXFP4, NVFP4 and FP8
summary: Staging sleep on a wearable device keeps the raw electroencephalogram (EEG) private and saves the energy needed to transmit it. It also requires small, energy-efficient neural networks. We benchmark 13 post-training quantization (PTQ) configurations, from FP16 to the block-scaled 4-bit formats MXFP4 and NVFP4, for five-stage sleep staging from single-channel Fpz-Cz EEG. We use Sleep-EDF-78 (78 subjects), subject-wise cross-validation, three training seeds, value-exact emulation, and per-subject paired statistics. All 8- and 16-bit formats stay within 0.45 percentage points (pp) of FP32 Macro-F1. With 4-bit weights and activations, an epoch-wise CNN loses 1.98 to 3.04 pp, and a temporal-context network loses at most 1.19 pp. A same-encoder ablation shows that temporal context explains little of this gap. At equal block size, NVFP4 outperforms MXFP4. The first layer, which quantizes the raw EEG, is the most sensitive layer in both networks. Keeping the first and last layers in FP8 brings both tested 4-bit formats within 0.48 pp of FP32. This recipe adds at most 2.1% weight storage, needs no retraining, and is equivalent to quantization-aware training (QAT) within an exploratory 1-pp margin. The 4-bit losses fall on the same subjects across architectures (Spearman correlation coefficient = 0.69 to 0.79), and they reduce N3 recall the most. On the nested Sleep-EDF-20 subset, NVFP4 with FP8 first and last layers again stays within 0.25 pp of FP32. Under MXFP4, however, the ranking of the architectures reverses, and FP8 first and last layers do not fully recover two of the three tested models. In our emulation, NVFP4 with FP8 first and last layers thus loses little accuracy without QAT in both cohorts.

title: JECT: Addressing the Context Shortcut in Joint-Embedding Predictive Learning for Chest CT
summary: Joint-embedding predictive architectures learn by predicting features of masked regions from visible context. In chest computed tomography, the findings that decide a diagnosis, such as a small nodule, are often not predictable from the surrounding anatomy. A hidden finding is then best predicted toward normal anatomy, and the prediction loss stops rewarding the encoder for representing it. We call this the context shortcut. Conditioning the predictor on the radiology report repairs the prediction, but in our setup the encoder gains little over image-only pretraining: the report supplies what the encoder never had to learn. JECT therefore gives the report two roles: a condition for the predictor and, through masked section-text prediction, a target for the encoder, which must predict the report's anatomical sections from the unmasked scan. A hierarchical three-dimensional encoder that predicts at every stage keeps this clinical content at every scale. In ablations, the text target improves classification and localization, while conditioning adds little to the encoder. Trained from scratch on 173k volumes, the recipe reaches the level of current computed tomography foundation models in classification, retrieval and nodule malignancy, and of task-specific models in lung-cancer risk prediction after fine-tuning. Conditioning still matters: its predictor can be reused, with no extra training, to show where a report sentence acts, changing most at the finding the sentence describes. Code and pretrained weights are available.

title: JevBench: Metamorphic Coherence Testing for Typed Probabilistic Decision Models
summary: Typed probabilistic decision models return distributions over specified answers, such as yes or no, a set of options or levels on an ordered scale. We ask whether their probabilities remain coherent when questions about the same input are reworded, negated, combined, given different options or placed in different batches. JevBench tests this coherence without gold labels. Its 50 metamorphic relations each test one law of probability or choice across five dimensions: representation, batch independence, probability measure, logical order and choice-set conditioning. Each test changes the question or batch while keeping the input fixed. Every model receives the same requests, fixed in advance. JevBench-240 contains 12,000 tests across 240 synthetic cases in 12 decision domains. A fixed subset of 1,200 tests, JevBench-mini, closely reproduces the full-suite ranking (Spearman 0.983). Across 21 openly released models, coherence scores range from 56.5 to 83.9. Batch independence holds for most models. Additivity fails broadly, particularly for complements, where the probabilities of a proposition and its negation should sum to one. A uniform reference model ignores the input and scores 89.4 at chance accuracy, exceeding every evaluated model's coherence score. Among decoders, accuracy ranges from 82.4% to 89.2%, while coherence ranges from 64.2 to 83.9. These results show why both measures are needed to assess decision models. JevBench is available as an open-source Python package.

title: Joint Classification and Generation on Tabular Data: an Empirical Study
summary: Many applications of machine learning on tabular data need both a classifier and a generator of realistic records. The default is to train two separate models, whereas a single joint model promises both from one set of weights. Several families of tabular deep learning models can be turned into such a joint model, which raises the question of which joint model is preferable at which computational budget. In this empirical study, we introduce and compare joint models based on four state-of-the-art tabular data modeling families (energy-based models, probabilistic circuits, tabular foundation models and tabular diffusion models) against measured FLOPs and wall-clock time, on 29 classification datasets. Methods are evaluated based on two defined aggregate scores that take into account different aspects of prediction and generation. We then also compare these joint models with every pair of a separate classifier and generator at different computational budgets, to see when a joint model may be a defendible choice against the regular practice of keeping a separate classifier and generator. We find that the best joint model is a probabilistic circuit at the smallest budgets and, beyond that, a tabular foundation model that generates column by column using a regressor (TabICL). Compared with pairs of separate models, this study finds a joint model is rarely preferable but often very close to the best pair, without the hassle of training and maintaining two separate models.

title: Joint Detection of Constructive Speech, Hate Speech and Agreement in Online Conversations
summary: Online hate speech is an ever-growing issue with negative impacts on both groups and individuals, potentially causing users to withdraw from online conversations and debate. With some prominent social media platforms reducing their moderation efforts, constructive speech has emerged as an alternative strategy for countering hate. Automated detection of constructive and hateful speech can aid monitoring and improve understanding of their prevalence and online dynamics. In this work, we collect and annotate a large dataset of English and Danish social media comments for hateful tone, constructive tone, and agreement with parent comments. We fine-tune several multilingual LLMs to classify along these three dimensions and compare context-enriched and non-context-enriched model architectures. The E5-large LLM performs best on both the context-enriched (82% average F1) and non-context-enriched (81.6% average F1) classification tasks, demonstrating the potential of multilingual LLMs for scalable detection of hateful and constructive speech across languages.

title: KKT Atlas: Learning Low-Dimensional Local Scenario Models for Contextual Stochastic Optimization
summary: In contextual stochastic optimization, integrated learning trains conditional models on operational loss, but repeatedly solving stochastic programs with many scenarios is costly. We propose KKT Atlas, which partitions contexts into local charts and identifies a low-dimensional subspace per chart from decision gradients of the scenario cost. It generates shared scenarios by jointly fitting subspace coordinates and context-dependent probabilities. We show that one more scenario than the subspace dimension suffices to approximate the conditional Karush-Kuhn-Tucker optimality condition under regularity conditions, yielding decision and risk bounds under local strong convexity, with generalization error scaling with the compact parameter dimension. On three synthetic problems, Atlas uses 4-18 scenarios per decision versus 500 for direct-solve full-support integrated learning. It attains comparable or lower risk with about $4$-$23\times$ construction and $13$-$61\times$ batch deployment speedups. Atlas also achieves lower risk than clustering-based reduction at matched support budgets. In real-world European grid reserve commitment, Atlas compresses 728 scenarios to 8-9, cutting construction and deployment times by factors of about 4 and 3 relative to full-support integrated learning. Its loss is lowest over 11 quarters and, over 17 later quarters with fixed settings, slightly higher than with full-support integrated learning and significantly lower than with the remaining benchmarks.

title: KiRA: Kronecker Input-Gated Rank Adaptation for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning of Pretrained Models
summary: Full fine-tuning of large pretrained models is expensive, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) is the standard alternative. Most PEFT methods use low-rank updates, whose rank lies far below that of full fine-tuning and is the same for every input. Input-adaptive variants vary the capacity per input but remain within the low-rank bottleneck, and whether a task benefits from input conditioning is not known before training. This paper introduces Kronecker input-gated rank adaptation (KiRA). Instead of the conventional low-rank product, the update $ΔW$ is the Kronecker product of a frozen random $p\times p$ matrix $A$ and a trainable factor $M(x)$, which overcomes the rank ceiling: because rank is multiplicative under this product, $A$ multiplies the rank of $M(x)$ by $p$ without adding trainable parameters. The factor $M(x)$ is further decomposed as $B_1\,\mathrm{diag}(g(x))\,B_2$, where the input gate $g(x)$, computed once per sample by a network shared across all adapted layers, adjusts the rank of the update to each input in steps of $p$. Where input conditioning is unnecessary, the gate is folded into $B_1$ at deployment. Because the gate changes the rank only in discrete steps, the benefit of input conditioning can be predicted before training from a few hundred labeled inputs. Across six medical imaging and language benchmarks, KiRA attains the highest mean score against five published baselines with 8.7--9.7 times fewer trainable parameters than low-rank adaptation, and the pre-training criterion agrees with the measured benefit of input conditioning on all six tasks.

title: Know When to Abstain: Conformal Confidence Estimation for Text-to-SQL
summary: Text-to-SQL systems often return queries that execute successfully but answer the wrong question. Detecting these errors at deployment is hard because execution correctness is defined against a gold query, which exists only in labeled data. We formulate confidence estimation for Text-to-SQL as probabilistic query validation under a latent correctness variable that is observable at calibration time through gold-SQL execution and latent at deployment. Our estimator separates generation from validation. A generator LLM writes and executes the query, and a different critic LLM judges the query and its execution result. The critic's validation and execution-grounded alignment scores are fused with the generator's verbalized confidence, token-level uncertainty, and SQL-structural features in a Random Forest, using two sequential LLM calls. Two calibration steps give finite-sample guarantees. A Learn-then-Test threshold ensures, with probability $1-δ$, that the error rate among accepted queries stays below a user-chosen budget. A conformal p-value bounds the false abstention rate. On Spider we use GPT-OSS-120B as generator and Gemma-4-31B as critic. The estimator obtains an AUARC of 0.899. Without abstention, 22.6% of queries are wrong. With a 15% risk budget ($δ=0.1$), a threshold is certified on all 10 resampled splits, and the system accepts 52.4% of queries on average with 9.1% observed error. Five different critic models give similar results. In a controlled comparison on Spider with Olmo-3-32B as generator, the estimator obtains an AUARC of 89.5, compared with 81.2 for the strongest logit-based baseline. Applied to BIRD without retraining, the confidence scores remain informative (AUROC 0.72, against 0.79 on Spider), but the risk guarantee does not transfer, as expected without exchangeability.

title: LATEC: Learned Axial TEnsor Compression for High-Dimensional Scientific Data
summary: With the growing scale of scientific simulation and infrastructure, part of the burden has shifted from producing scientific data to analyzing and storing it. Compression is a key step to expanding storage capacity, but requires dedicated techniques to enforce user-specified pointwise error bounds that ensure the validity of downstream scientific workflows. To further push the limits of compression, novel learned codecs have been developed, in particular for images and videos, but these methods often optimize for aggregated distortion and fail to meet error bound standards. Moreover, these methods often target fixed field dimensionality, failing to account for many scientific data use cases, or at the expense of large adaptation or retraining costs. In this work, we introduce the Learned Axial TEnsor Compression (LATEC) method, an error-bounded codec with a dimension-agnostic learned predictor based on a GNN architecture. LATEC is pretrained on synthetic 2-D and 4-D fields, and evaluated with and without domain fine-tuning on 13 scientific fields in 3-D to 5-D. Results show that LATEC is consistently competitive with SZ3, achieving an 18.1% average improvement and greater consistency across all domains than other compressors. These results demonstrate that a shared learned predictor can serve as a single error-bounded codec across tensor dimensionalities, competitive with specialized compressors, while retaining pointwise error guarantees.

title: LEGOSpec: A Composable and Efficient Framework for Speculative Draft Design and Training
summary: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model (LLM) generation using a lightweight draft. Existing methods evaluate complete recipes under different training configurations, leaving component effects, interactions, and composition benefits unclear. Therefore, we present LEGOSpec, a composable framework for speculative draft design and training. LEGOSpec decomposes draft models into Context, Backbone, Proposal, and Objective components that share a unified training infrastructure. Using LEGOSpec, we systematically vary components and evaluate selected combinations under matched training conditions to isolate their effects and interactions. These experiments reveal three findings: (1) Different workloads favor different backbones, depending on context length and memory budget, with within-block dependency modeling particularly important for long contexts. (2) Proposal design must balance acceptance and latency. (3) The training objective should match token distributions locally and optimize acceptance length across the block. These findings guide workload-aware configurations and DFlux, a balanced general-purpose draft combining a convolution-equipped SWA--GQA hybrid backbone, Residual Corrector, and hierarchical supervision. Across Qwen and Gemma models, DFlux improves acceptance length over the strongest baseline by up to 13.7% on regular benchmarks and 34.7% on long-context workloads. To support efficient training, LEGOSpec integrates metadata-aware scheduling and asynchronous execution, increasing training throughput by up to 79% and accelerating offline supervision preparation by up to $3.11\times$ over SpecForge.

title: LIBRA: Runtime Co-Tuning of Batch Size and Parallelism for Time-Efficient LLM Training
summary: Training large language models (LLMs) requires choosing both a batch size and a parallel configuration. Existing systems make these decisions in isolation, tuning parallelism for throughput and batch size for convergence, but neither objective alone determines training efficiency. We present LIBRA, a lightweight runtime framework that co-tunes batch size and parallel configuration to minimize end-to-end time. LIBRA treats throughput and convergence as two noisy objectives and searches their joint space using parallel noisy expected hypervolume improvement (qNEHVI). To make this runtime search efficient, we propose hierarchical pruning, which removes infeasible and low-throughput parallel configurations through system-level performance estimation and then narrows batch-size candidates through critical-batch-size-aware convergence monitoring. We further design acquisition-guided parallel evaluation (AGPE), which evaluates surviving candidates concurrently across GPU groups in order of their acquisition values. On clusters of up to 256 GPUs, LIBRA reduces time-to-convergence by 31.1% on average over state-of-the-art methods, while runtime tuning accounts for only 0.3-3.5% of overall time.

title: LLM Agent Authorization Across Context Compaction
summary: Request-derived authorizers such as Progent protect LLM agents from prompt injection by deriving what an agent may do from the user's request. Their guarantee rests on attribution: the request is taken to be what the user said. Compaction breaks it. At every automatic compaction we observed, Claude Code and Codex placed a model-written summary of earlier turns as a user message, so the compactor's quotation of the user, documents and injected text reads as the user speaking. Because a policy frozen at the first request lets the agent finish few later tasks, we let Progent derive its policy for each request, and find that what it grants then follows what the compactor wrote. Even a payee the user stated is not safe: when an attacker's notice states another account as plain data and the user asks to pay the rent, the policy derived from a frontier compactor's summary admits the notice's account in 91% of cases, and the one derived from the user's own words in none. The cause is general: we prove that an authorizer that cannot see who wrote which bytes cannot treat a forged record differently from the legitimate one it imitates by more than the two are distinguishable, and that the bound is tight. Frontier compactors bear this out: they mark injected instructions, which have no legitimate twin, but rarely injected data, which does. What a compactor keeps, and how it marks it, is a security parameter. The fix follows from attribution: the authorizer credits only what the user said, authenticated on arrival and carried verbatim across the boundary, while the agent still reads the summary. We prove that it then receives exactly that text or nothing, so an attacker can block the policy but cannot shape it, and adaptive attacks on our implementation confirm it. In 40 attacked AgentDojo episodes re-run with the fix, no attacker action completes while the agent reads the summary.

title: LRQ-Cache: Compressing Feature Caches in Video Diffusion via Low-Rank Approximation and Quantization
summary: Video diffusion transformers (DiTs) achieve high-fidelity generation, but inference is expensive because every denoising step evaluates a large transformer over all spatiotemporal tokens of the video. Temporal caching accelerates them by reusing intermediate features across denoising steps. However, retaining dense feature tensors introduces a persistent storage cost that grows with video length, resolution, and cache coverage, reaching 109-346 GiB per video for the predictive caches we evaluate. Such states exceed the memory of a single GPU, so native caches must either be offloaded to the CPU, which slows generation, or be sharded across several GPUs, e.g., with sequence parallelism, so that the cache rather than the compute sets the number of GPUs. We instead shrink the cached state itself, exploiting its redundancy: a few channel patterns shared across tokens capture much of the energy of each cached feature. Based on this observation, we propose LRQ-Cache, a training-free method that combines low-rank approximation and quantization for feature-cache compression. LRQ-Cache represents each cached feature with a small set of factors, quantizes them before storage, and reconstructs the feature at reuse time, leaving cache mechanisms unchanged. Across three caching mechanisms on HunyuanVideo and Wan2.1, LRQ-Cache reduces the persistent state of predictive caches by 42-71x, to 2.3-4.9 GiB per video. VBench stays within 0.25 pp of the native cache for TeaCache, and the larger drops of the Wan2.1 predictive caches, up to 3.5 pp, shrink at higher ranks. As a result, predictive caches that exceed the memory of a single 80 GB H100 GPU fit on it with LRQ-Cache, making generation 2.7-5.9x faster than with CPU-offloaded native caches.

title: LUCID: Statistically Grounded Self-Correction for LLM Reasoning Evaluation
summary: Cheap language-model raters grade chain-of-thought reasoning at scale, yet systematic step-rating errors can skew reasoning audits and solution rankings. We introduce LUCID (Loop for Unbiased Calibration via Inference-time Diagnosis), which pairs prompt self-correction with Design-based Supervised Learning (DSL). Without retraining or weight access, LUCID calibrates binary step ratings by aligning predicted and expert soundness rates. From a small expert-labeled set, LUCID summarizes rater bias in plain text and prompts the rater to re-grade unseen steps. For example, on PRM800K, GPT-5-mini grades too strictly, under-rating computation, verification, and late-trace steps most acutely. In one pass, LUCID shrinks GPT-5-mini's calibration gap from 7.8 to 0.9 percentage points in absolute predicted-expert rate difference. LUCID also halves false alarms (sound steps rated unsound) and lifts error-detection F1 on unsound steps by 32%. LUCID retains these gains with 1,000 diagnostic steps or overall-gap feedback alone. The loop also transfers across models and domains: it applies GPT-5-mini's bias profile to lift GLM-5.2's PRM800K accuracy, and it narrows calibration gaps for overly strict but capable raters across math, science, web, and logic benchmarks. Because prompt feedback shifts thresholds without improving class-balanced sound/unsound discrimination, LUCID filters re-grading with pre-/post-checks that skip already calibrated raters and roll back ineffective passes. Finally, we reuse that expert set with raw corpus ratings in DSL for calibration and regression debiasing, and apply DSL to pair-labeled steps for sound-step transitions. DSL's out-of-fold soundness probabilities lift best-of-K selection to match expert labels, while its doubly-robust estimators beat expert-only regression fits at small budgets and cut sound-step transition error by nearly two-thirds.

title: Label leakage through file headers: geometry and batch confounds in public mammography datasets, and a pre-training acceptance gate
summary: A dataset whose diagnostic label can be recovered from non-diagnostic information yields high, reproducible and uninformative model performance. We applied pre-training controls that see only image geometry, global texture, a sub-collection identifier or one covariate to six public mammography datasets, against a stop threshold of AUC 0.60. In KAU-BCMD, geometry alone predicted the BI-RADS class at AUC 1.0000 in a local copy and at a mean of 0.979 in a public Kaggle archive; after resizing, texture alone gave 0.847. In CMMD, the sub-collection prefix predicted malignancy at 0.7753; the restricted sub-collection passed geometry (0.5000) and texture (0.5810) but failed an identifier-order control added post hoc (test AUC 0.9926). CBIS-DDSM exceeded the stop on geometry (pooled mean 0.654 over 20 splits), a verdict statistic chosen post hoc; its official mass and calcification splits did not. M-SYNTH, INbreast and a partial VinDr-Mammo copy passed the few controls run. We release the code and derived tables. There is no quantum component in the inference path.

title: Language Models Steer on Injected Uncertainty Tokens, but Fail to Self-Monitor In Situ
summary:
Prompting language models to verbalize stepwise numerical confidence during generation is an increasingly popular approach for triggering backtracking and error correction in agentic reasoning. This strategy presupposes two capabilities: (1) in-situ monitoring fidelity (does confidence drop when an error occurs?) and (2) downstream steering control (does an uncertainty token causally steer the model to repair its error?). We evaluated four open-weights models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, and Phi-4, 14.7B) across 15,200 math benchmark attempts, isolating 2,017 reasoning errors within each model's capability frontier. Applying 27,568 counterfactual continuations across these failure points, we demonstrate a consistent decoupling between monitoring and control.
  On monitoring, all four models fail to detect their own errors. Verbalized confidence does not distinguish mistake steps from sound reasoning, yielding near-chance within-position AUROCs between 0.500 and 0.561. Even at a model's first reasoning error, trajectory confidence remains saturated at 95.1% to 99.9%, with noticeable drops ($\ge 10$ points) appearing on fewer than 9% of errors in Llama and under 1.6% in the other three models. In contrast, models respond readily to external uncertainty: injecting a low-confidence tag (10%) at the error step significantly increases downstream correction across all models (+3.7 to +22.5 points over format-matched 95% certainty; all $p \le 0.0022$), reaching up to 38.5% under active rethinking instructions. However, injecting doubt onto already-correct steps causes models to discard valid reasoning, reducing solve rates by up to 22.8 points. Inference-time self-correction is thus bottlenecked by in-situ error detection rather than downstream repair capacity: models readily steer toward recovery when prompted with doubt, yet fail to self-monitor during generation.

title: Latent Channel Completion for Forecasting in Sensor Networks with Failed Detectors
summary: Monitoring networks for traffic and utility infrastructure lose sensors routinely, and forecasting models that couple sensors together to gain accuracy also inherit an exposure to those losses. When a detector stops reporting, the substituted value is embedded as though it were a reading and propagates through the shared representation that couples the network, degrading forecasts for sensors that are still healthy. Because these models are selected on benchmarks where every sensor reports, the exposure is absent from the numbers used to choose them. We introduce Latent Channel Completion, a channel-axis joint embedding predictive objective that reconstructs missing sensors' latent representations rather than their values, since a coupling operator consumes embeddings and never sees raw readings. Channels are masked during training and their representations predicted from surviving channels against stop-gradient targets; at inference the operator fills in whichever sensors the monitoring system reports as dark, using parameters shared with the forecaster. On three highway detector networks, after half of each network goes dark, the accuracy advantage of coupling changes by -1.0, -0.5 and +8.8 percentage points, against losses of 10.2 to 50.3 points for the unmodified forecaster, which on one network falls behind an uncoupled reference entirely. Against cross-channel ridge imputation drawing on the same surviving sensors, completing the latent lowers error by a further 13.9% and 28.6%, and on complete inputs, the method matches its backbone. The benefit tracks how much a network gains from coupling when intact, giving operators a criterion evaluable before any outage occurs.

title: Latent Class Mixed Model Variational Autoencoders for Scalable Phenotyping of Health Trajectories
summary: Clustering longitudinal health trajectories requires handling high-dimensional measurements, irregular visit times, and subject-level heterogeneity while retaining clinically interpretable structure. Existing methods address this only partially: latent-class mixed models yield an interpretable, covariate-driven partition but do not scale past a handful of markers, while deep time-series clustering scales at the cost of that structure and generally requires a common time grid. We introduce the Latent Class Mixed Model Variational Autoencoder (LCMM-VAE), a deep generative model whose latent prior is a mixture of class-specific linear mixed models, so that each subject's latent trajectory decomposes into its class mean trajectory and a subject-specific deviation. We derive a variational EM algorithm whose class responsibilities, random effects and mixed-model parameters are updated in closed form, and provide identifiability guarantees under stated conditions. Experiments on simulated and real longitudinal cohorts show that LCMM-VAE returns a partition, a reconstruction of incomplete trajectories and interpretable class-level dynamics at once, while remaining competitive with classical and deep baselines.

title: Latent Merger: Latent-Space Composition of Hypernetwork-Generated LoRAs
summary: Recent work proposes hypernetworks that convert a document into a low-rank parameter update (LoRA) in a single forward pass, enabling fast injection of new knowledge into a frozen LLM. However, storing separate LoRA adapters for each document can be unsustainable in streaming settings. In this paper, we study the problem of composing hypernetwork-generated LoRAs using two representative systems, Doc-to-LoRA and SHINE. We show that hypernetwork-generated LoRAs have a geometry sharply different from directly fine-tuned LoRAs. They exhibit greater spectral concentration and stronger cross-document alignment than next-token prediction and QA fine-tuned adapters, which are diffuse and nearly orthogonal across documents. Guided by this observation, we propose latent-space LoRA merging. We compose the intermediate hypernetwork latents and then decode the merged latent through the frozen LoRA-generation head. We show that latent-space merging techniques consistently improve over weight-space and factor-space baselines while preserving a single fixed-rank adapter. These results support latent-space composition as a promising mechanism for combining hypernetwork-generated LoRAs under a fixed output-rank budget.

title: LatentLens: Rethinking Latent Interface in Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Latent interfaces let agents in a multi-agent system communicate through continuous representations rather than decoded text. Prior work reports performance and efficiency gains, but neither separates latent communication from the agent harness nor examines its internal components, leaving its actual contribution unclear. We propose LatentLens, a framework that decouples the latent interface at two levels: externally from the agent harness, to measure its contribution to overall performance (RQ1), and internally into realignment compatibility, information accessibility, and propagation dynamics, to identify the benefits and limitations of each (RQ2). Across seven benchmarks with Qwen3 models, adding the latent interface to the same harness does not improve and can even substantially degrade accuracy. Internally, latent representations retain some domain information, but incompatible realignment can substantially degrade performance, and repeated latent steps can amplify representation-level failures. Thus, while latent representations may preserve information, they do not necessarily ensure effective communication, which also requires compatible realignment, information accessibility, and stable propagation.

title: Lazy Agents Answer Against Their Own Beliefs: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Beliefs Teaches Them to Act on What They Believe
summary: AI agents working on long tasks often commit to an answer before they have enough evidence, a behavior called laziness. In our evaluations, they frequently commit even while their stated belief still names several possible answers. An outcome reward at the end of the episode scores only the final answer, so it cannot teach the agent when to commit, because a lucky guess receives the same reward as an answer backed by evidence. During training, however, the simulator can compute the exact posterior over the answer at every step and tell whether the evidence is already enough. We propose Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Beliefs (RLVB), which rewards the agent for taking further steps while this posterior still allows several answers and for committing once the evidence is sufficient. The reward needs no judge, critic or reward model, and it never reads the belief line the agent writes before each action. We also introduce Pro Worlds, a benchmark of visual puzzles where the agent views a large world through a small window. We evaluate three vision-language models on three benchmarks, two of which are never seen in training. RLVB improves the base model in all nine settings, by 17.1% on average. Under the outcome reward, GRPO and PPO fall below the base model on average. RLVB also outperforms PPO with a process reward from an LLM judge by 9.3% on average while using 1.6 times fewer GPU-hours. The trained agent answers with sufficient evidence in 51%, 12% and 74% of the episodes on the three benchmarks, against 8%, 0.4% and 36% for the base model. Its accuracy gain therefore comes from answering more often at high levels of evidence. The belief line shows how the agent reaches this evidence: it acts on its own belief. It commits at only 0.1 to 2.2% of the turns at which the evidence is insufficient and its line still names several answers, against 3 to 68% for the base model.

title: LeJEPA Features Are Not Isotropic, and Should Not Be
summary: The SIGReg term in LeJEPA regularizes features to have an isotropic Gaussian distribution. Our first result is to show that this regularizer, in practice, cannot achieve its goal. We design a modified regularizer to enforce the objective better. This leads to slightly improved performance. For example, on ImageNet-100, our modified regularizer reaches the final accuracy of SIGReg in 1.3$\times$ fewer epochs. Our second result argues that self-supervised encoders should not have isotropic Gaussian features. We show that the alignment term in LeJEPA conflicts with SIGReg, because it couples the magnitude of the features with their directions. In contrast, isotropic Gaussian features would entail independent magnitude and directions. Features obtained with LeJEPA are, in fact, not isotropic. So LeJEPA has two issues. Its regularizer is weak, and the isotropic Gaussian target is too strict. Our third result is about reformulating the isotropic Gaussian regularizer to enforce only the marginal distributions of the magnitude and direction, without enforcing independence. This leads to a simple regularization term, PolarReg, that can be optimized reliably across many different datasets, batch sizes and embedding dimensions without any hyper-parameter changes. On ImageNet-1k, our technique matches the accuracy of LeJEPA and its variants in 4.7$\times$ fewer epochs. It improves the final accuracy by 1.8 points.

title: Leaks by Installments: Cross-Session Answer Disclosure in LLM Tutors and a Ledger-Based Defense
summary: Tutors built on large language models (LLMs) are told not to give away answers, but a learner does not have to ask for the answer all at once. Existing safeguards judge each reply within the current conversation, so a learner can open a new session, reword the problem, or request a worked solution to the same problem with different numbers. We call this cross-session disclosure and propose a defense: a persistent, per-learner disclosure ledger. For every problem a learner brings, the system builds a typed solution graph. Before a reply is released, a gate matches the reply's own content, not the learner's wording, against the ledger by result values and by type-labeled solution structure, then computes which steps the learner could now derive. The reply is withheld if that set reaches the final answer or exceeds a budget. In a simulation of 3,000 problems, the ledger reduced leakage through renumbered practice variants from 100% to 10.6% while honest learners completed 94-99.5% of problems. With two real LLM tutors (Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and Phi-3.5-mini-instruct) on 60 problems, leakage through renumbered variants fell from 0.58 to 0.08 and from 1.00 to 0.18, with 98% honest completion. The ledger did not reduce split requests beyond a per-session gate in the live runs. All acceptance criteria were fixed before each run.

title: Learning Compact State Abstractions for LLM Agents
summary: LLM agents commonly use the full interaction history as a proxy for state, retaining all past observations and actions regardless of whether they remain relevant. We instead ask what information an agent actually needs to carry forward. We define agent state as a compact abstraction of interaction history that preserves the competence of a fixed reference agent, with the minimal such abstraction as the ideal. Because matching the reference agent's behavior is unnecessarily restrictive and difficult for black-box policies, we define sufficiency through task performance rather than behavior matching. We represent state abstractions as deterministic recursive programs and search over them using an LLM-guided genetic algorithm. Across ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, the learned abstractions preserve near-reference task success while reducing mean policy input by up to 71% and 57%, respectively. The resulting programs are directly inspectable, providing an explicit account of what information is retained, updated, and discarded during interaction.

title: Learning Neurovascular Codes for EEG-to-fMRI Synthesis
summary: In this paper, we introduce Neurovascular Codes as shared EEG representations for fMRI generation. We first train a separate EEG encoder to predict each fMRI signal, learning target-specific temporal and spectral features from the same EEG window. After training, we freeze the encoders and project their concatenated hidden features into a shared neurovascular code. Conditioned on this code, stochastic interpolant transforms Gaussian noise into a vector of fMRI signals, allowing different responses to be sampled for the same EEG window. We evaluate our approach on eight public simultaneous EEG-fMRI datasets, including four resting-state and four task-based datasets with 61,646 volume-level pairs. Under within-subject and held-out-subject evaluation, our model improves average Pearson correlation over the strongest encoder baselines by 19.1% and 19.8%, respectively. The corresponding improvements over the strongest generator baselines are 18.8% and 47.9%. Beyond reconstruction accuracy, we also evaluate the generated signals using subject-identification classifiers trained on real fMRI. Our method achieves the highest mean accuracy among the evaluated generators. We hope that our work opens up new opportunities for cross-modal brain modeling.

title: Learning What vs. Learning How: Decomposing Task and Interface Competence in Agentic Training
summary: LLM agents operate through harnesses that define system prompts, action formats, feedback loops, and resource constraints. A model may possess the knowledge needed to solve a task yet fail to express that knowledge through a particular harness. This raises a basic question: when a policy fails under a given harness, is it missing task knowledge or the competence to operate the interface? We distinguish two components of agentic competence: task competence, the knowledge and reasoning needed to solve a task, and interface competence, the ability to act on that knowledge through a given harness. Across four reasoning and agentic benchmarks, we show that harness-conditioned training yields vastly different outcomes depending on how these interact. Multi-harness distillation aggregates task knowledge from trajectories collected through different harnesses into a shared policy, but this knowledge is realised only when training preserves or improves competence on the inference-time interface. Otherwise, single-harness training can induce interference in interface competence, sometimes catastrophically collapsing performance on a held-out harness despite improvements in underlying task knowledge. To disentangle task and interface supervision, we introduce harness rehearsal: distillation on traces that carry minimal task knowledge while exercising the target interface. Cross-harness task supervision or rehearsal alone yields little gain, but their combination yields gains far larger than either: on BFCL V3 multi-turn with Qwen3-4B, they achieve 8.5% and 32.5% respectively, versus 58.8% together. Finally, on-policy reinforcement learning (RL) is more robust than distillation to single-harness training: it does not substantially degrade performance on other harnesses, and interface competence acquired through multi-harness distillation persists through subsequent RL.

title: Learning the Platform, Not the Learner: Sequencing Shortcuts in the Offline Evaluation of Educational Recommender Systems and LLM Rankers
summary: Educational recommenders are usually compared offline, by how well they predict the next activity in logs of tutoring systems, learning applications and MOOCs, where the next activity is largely decided by the platform: teachers assign problem sets, tutors draw problems until mastery, engines select questions. On eight public datasets from five platforms, we compare four structural predictors, which use nothing about the learner beyond the last activity, with ten personalised recommenders and with open-weight LLM rankers from 0.5 to 7 billion parameters, under two protocols. The structural predictors reach between 0.81 and 1.00 of the best accuracy of any method (median 0.95), mostly through population transitions rather than the course order; the best personalised recommender is significantly better on five datasets, by 0.007 to 0.102 NDCG@10, and on Eedi in three of four training runs. Every method is far less accurate on steps along transitions never seen in training and on steps chosen by learners. LLM rankers look competent with random negatives but are never much better than a word-matching baseline, and with negatives that are plausible under the course structure they stay close to random or well behind the transition heuristic, whatever their size. In a simulation with known learner needs, the structural share tracks the share of steps decided by the platform, and offline accuracy ranks an oracle of the learners' needs below imitators of the platform. Weighting test steps by how unlikely the structure makes them restores much of the link with usefulness and, on the real data, reveals a significant personalisation signal on seven of the eight datasets. We propose a syllabus-aware evaluation checklist and release a Python package that reports the lift of any recommender over the structure.

title: Let The Pixels Through: Rethinking Long Skip Connections for Scalable Pixel Diffusion
summary: Training pixel diffusion models remains less straightforward, owing to the ad hoc training recipes and architecture designs, along with the sensitivity to hyper-parameter choices. We show that strong denoisers can be built by refining existing pixel-native designs from the literature. Specifically, we revisit the long skip connection in U-Net and find that the optimization benefit commonly attributed to it is not necessary for its denoising benefit. We further find that the conventional linear combination of features from the skip and main backbone is inadequate for regimes of various noise levels. Motivated by these observations, we introduce two core modifications. First, we adopt asymmetric long skips, which propagate fine-grained information from input embeddings to decoder layers. Second, we introduce adaGLU, a SwiGLU-like MLP block, in decoder layers to adaptively filter information from the embeddings before being added to main-branch features. The above designs give a simple pixel diffusion transformer architecture. When trained from scratch, it scales smoothly from small-scale baselines up to 1.6B parameters, achieving 1.62 and 1.70 FID on ImageNet-256 and -512, respectively. Besides, it natively supports multimodal inputs, such as text and images, yielding competitive performance in text-to-image generation. We release our codes at https://github.com/AMAP-ML/PiT

title: Let Vision-Language Models Generate Images through Their Representations
summary: Recent unified multimodal models aim to combine visual understanding and generation within a single model, yet effectively integrating the two capabilities remains challenging. Leveraging pretrained vision-language models offers a way to build on already learned multimodal knowledge, but making this knowledge effectively accessible to visual generation remains nontrivial. We find that a central challenge lies in the heterogeneous visual representations used for understanding and generation. To address this challenge, we introduce Integral, which converts a pretrained vision-language model into a unified multimodal model by constructing a shared visual representation space across the two capabilities. Integral implements this design through two complementary components. Abstraction Fusion constructs shared visual tokens by aggregating hierarchical representations from the frozen vision encoder, while Block-wise MoT introduces a lightweight generative stream that interacts with the vision-language model only at block boundaries. Our approach effectively preserves the pretrained understanding capability while extending it to strong visual generation. Controlled comparisons further demonstrate that sharing visual representations between understanding and generation substantially improves generative learning compared with using a separate visual representation space, despite comparable reconstruction fidelity. These results suggest that representations learned by pretrained vision-language models already provide an effective foundation for visual generation.

title: LimoBench: How Street Smart Are Large Language Models?
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have transformed how humans interact with information, enabling natural-language interfaces across various domains. They are increasingly deployed for geospatial applications including map-based question answering, location-based services, and natural-language interfaces to spatial databases. But are LLMs truly location-aware, able to reliably interpret and precisely answer location queries involving real-world coordinates, points of interest (POIs), and geospatial distances? To answer this concretely, we present LimoBench, a street-level benchmark of 82 natural-language location queries over seven canonical spatial operations: geocoding, reverse geocoding, routing, directionality, range search, $k$-nearest-neighbor search, and spatial join. The queries are grounded in real map data of West Lafayette, Indiana, and are graded by location and semantic complexity. They are designed to probe LLMs' street-level spatial awareness, from simple lookups to multi-step spatial reasoning. We also present Limo, an approach based on the Model Context Protocol (MCP) that enhances the location awareness of LLMs. Limo grounds LLMs in PostGIS-backed spatial data through a compact set of tools. We find that ungrounded models mostly achieve single-digit accuracy (3.1% for GPT-6 Luna) across different spatial operations. In contrast, the same models achieve near-perfect accuracy (99.3% for GPT-6 Luna) when given access to Limo's spatial tools through MCP. Current LLMs thus have limited and unreliable street-level spatial knowledge, while grounding provides accurate answers at modest overhead (+0.2 s latency, 7.7$\times$ tokens, and 2.2$\times$ cost for GPT-6 Luna). We release the benchmark, Limo toolset, and evaluation code to encourage the community to evaluate their own location-aware LLM approaches.

title: LineEX: Data Extraction from Scientific Line Charts
summary: In this paper, we introduce LINEEX that extracts data from scientific line charts. We adapt existing vision transformers and pose detection methods and showcase significant performance gains over existing SOTA baselines. We also propose a new loss function and present its effectiveness against existing loss functions. In addition, we synthetically created the largest line chart dataset comprising 430K images. The code is available at https://github.com/Shiva-sankaran/LineEX.

title: Linear Probes Can Guide: Training-Free Control of Representation Generators
summary: Representation-space generative models, such as Representation Autoencoders (RAEs), leverage pretrained vision foundation models (VFMs) primarily to accelerate training and improve sample fidelity. Yet VFMs are more than reconstruction tokenizers, as they feature rich representation spaces that are highly organized and linearly readable. We observe that this removes a key obstacle of post-hoc guidance: by linearity of expectation, a clean probe applied to an ideal denoiser's prediction yields the exact posterior mean of the probe scores at any noise level. This regime, which we call Semantic Mean-Space, turns semantic guidance into a Bayesian linear inverse problem, bypassing the need for training-time conditioning. With this foundation, we propose LiSM, a unified framework for Linear Guidance in Semantic Mean-Space. To validate the framework, we developed and adapted different solvers, and characterized them based on how they estimate probe-space uncertainty and propagate the correction through the representation. In addition, we propose Fit-Path, a solver designed to achieve strong global and local control. Our results in four control setups (class, attributes, foreground, and keypoints) show that LiSM methods, and Fit-Path in particular, provide effective, lightweight control across global and local tasks, outperforming noise-aware and pixel-space guidance.

title: Lit Up but Not Needed: Scoped Lesions Show Where Multimodal Mixture-of-Experts Depend on Their Experts
summary: Cognitive neuroscience learned that an activation map is not a map of necessity. Regions that light up during a task are not always needed for it, and only lesions reveal which ones are. Mixture-of-experts (MoE) vision-language models come with an activation map for free, since the router records which experts respond to image and text tokens, and recent work reads modality-specialized experts off this map. We bring the lesion. In Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B, Kimi-VL-A3B and Gemma-4-26B-A4B, 3 to 12% of the experts are vision-exclusive: image tokens route to them at up to five times the uniform rate and text tokens almost never. In Qwen3-VL they receive a quarter of all image-token routing, and lesioning all of them costs less than one percentage point on average over eight perception benchmarks and free-form OCR, no more than lesioning a random set of the same size. In Kimi-VL and Gemma-4 the lesion also costs no more than a random set. Scoped lesions, which remove an expert set only at image positions or only at text positions, then show where the models do depend on their experts. In Qwen3-VL, silencing every expert at every image position costs 3 points, against 45 at text positions, where the dependence sits in dual-use experts that text-only tasks need as well. Across models the image-side dependence is 2 to 3 points in Qwen3-VL and Kimi-VL and 26 in Gemma-4. Reading text in images is the one ability that needs image-position experts in every model. The exclusive experts receive informative patches, produce outputs of ordinary size, and stay inert under sensory deprivation: text-only training recruits them only when load balancing forces it. In Kimi-VL the balancing bias itself manufactures most of them. Load balancing draws the modality map in the part of the computation the models depend on least. Expert selection, pruning and skipping should follow the lesion, not the map.

title: LiteSTAR: Low-Rank Channel Modulation for Temporally Consistent CVD Video Compensation
summary: Color Vision Deficiency (CVD) affects a large population worldwide, yet practical recoloring must run continuously on-device. Frame-wise video recoloring produces color flickering, while existing methods rely on costly cross-frame alignment in pixel or feature space. We observe that color flickering correlates with variations in channel-wise responses, with color-sensitive variations concentrated in a low-rank subspace. Based on this observation, we propose Lightweight Spatio-Temporal Adaptive Recoloring (LiteSTAR), built around LiCaD, a plug-and-play Lightweight Channel-Adaptive Decoder. LiCaD performs temporal filtering in a low-rank state space with learned process and observation uncertainties. It then modulates feature channels to achieve temporal consistency without explicit spatial alignment. LiteSTAR further employs adaptive patch routing to improve color discrimination for CVD users while avoiding unnecessary over-enhancement. We also introduce EgoCVDSet, the first egocentric video benchmark for CVD recoloring. Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate that LiteSTAR achieves superior performance with only 0.05M parameters. LiCaD further demonstrates strong generalization across different tasks and network architectures. The code, models, and dataset will be released after review.

title: Load Balancing Neurons: Firing-Rate Control Sustains Plasticity in Continual Learning
summary: Neural networks in continual learning often lose plasticity: some neurons become inactive, while others fire almost constantly. This limits adaptation to shifting data and wastes capacity. Prior work mitigates this by periodically reinitializing low-utility units, but such resets can destroy previously learned features and do not proactively prevent low utility. We study a simple diagnostic measure: the firing rate of ReLU units, defined as the fraction of positive pre-activations. Low rates identify dead units, while very high rates indicate linearized, always-on units. Based on this view, we introduce a lightweight load-balancing mechanism that adjusts per-neuron thresholds to keep firing rates within a target range. Across continual ImageNet and class-incremental CIFAR-100, firing-rate distributions explain differences in plasticity across a range of approaches, including well-known techniques such as L2 regularization and non-affine normalization, and load balancing matches or exceeds reset-based methods on both benchmarks. The same mechanism carries over to reinforcement learning, improving Rainbow DQN on Atari over a LayerNorm baseline.

title: Longitudinal Characterization of Personalized Hydration Dynamics Using a Facial-Video Digital Hydration Biomarker
summary:
Background. Hydration is often assessed at a single time point despite continuous changes in body water. A facial-video biomarker has tracked hydration-state transitions, but its longitudinal behavior is unclear.
  Objective. To assess within-person hydration score changes, individual differences in fluid response, and implications for personal calibration.
  Methods. Five adults completed water and electrolyte days with an identical 2.0 L fluid schedule, using facial videos every 30 minutes over 12 hours (250 videos). On a separate morning, each completed a 500 mL electrolyte challenge with baseline and four follow-up videos over 2 hours (25 videos). Analyses assessed trajectories, post-drink changes, variability, time at or above score 50, and exploratory effects of starting score and beverage day.
  Results. The first scan was the day's lowest on 7 of 10 days. Across 50 intakes, the mean post-drink change was +4.0 points, exceeding a shuffled-time comparison (p less than 0.001). For 21 intakes starting below 50, no subsequent score fell; the mean rise was +11.3 points versus +5.7 expected under permutation (p less than 0.001). Intakes starting at 50 or above showed no rise beyond chance. After 500 mL electrolytes, mean change over 2 hours was positive for all five participants, with peak increases of 7.2 to 22.6 points at 30 to 90 minutes. Despite identical fluid schedules, time at or above 50 ranged from 16% to 100%. The electrolyte day showed a greater mean increase from morning baseline than the water day (+7.7 points), although day order was fixed.
  Conclusion. Facial-video hydration scores showed longitudinal changes associated with drinking and marked individual differences. These exploratory findings support further research on personal calibration and hydration protocols in larger controlled studies.

title: Look Before You Commit: Visual-Evidence-Guided Decoding for Multimodal Diffusion Language Models
summary: Diffusion multimodal large language models rely on confidence to decide when to commit candidate tokens during generation. In multimodal tasks, however, confidence cannot distinguish whether a candidate originates from image evidence or the language prior. We perform paired forward ablation and find that nearly nine out of ten high-confidence commits are insensitive to the image, while degenerate and hallucination samples exhibit significant increases in the entropy of deep-layer attention organization. Based on this diagnosis, we propose CD-APC, a training-free decoding method. CD-APC performs evidence-adjusted scoring within a base-supported pool and uses dual gating based on model acceptability and contrastive concentration to decide whether to commit, together with an inverse-window mechanism that adapts to inter-step difficulty. Across two backbones and five benchmarks, CD-APC consistently improves performance, indicating that stable visual evidence improves model outputs.

title: Look Where Camouflage Breaks: Concealment-Guided Observation for Camouflaged Object Detection
summary: A camouflaged object can blend into its surroundings at one scale and become distinguishable at another. Yet a region's apparent ambiguity gives limited guidance on which observation would resolve it. The challenge is to connect the form and scale of concealment to the evidence that a new view can reveal. We introduce CamoBreak, an active framework for camouflaged object detection guided by a Concealment Spectrum. From the image and current predictions, the spectrum measures regional resemblance and boundary ambiguity across comparison scales, distinguishing persistent concealment from separation emerging at finer or broader scales. These measurements guide crop selection from the already-captured image and recognition against global foreground and background references. An object-conditioned spatial preference then selects where local evidence should update the prediction and feature memory, retaining target corrections while suppressing background distractions. Accepted corrections reshape the next measurement, while predicted segmentation benefit determines whether to observe again. Experiments across encoder families and related segmentation tasks show consistent improvements. Targeted analyses support improved small-target recovery, multiple-object coverage, and selective evidence integration. Code will be released.

title: LookAnything: A Foundation Model for Holistic Gaze Following
summary: Human gaze provides a rich window into attention and intent, making its understanding essential for applications ranging from social signal analysis to human-robot interaction. Existing methods typically employ highly customized architectures relying on auxiliary inputs like head crops or depth maps, causing cascading errors and inference overhead. Trained on single domains and confined to isolated gaze following with heatmap outputs, they lack flexibility and generalization for diverse interactive scenarios. To bridge this gap, we present LookAnything, a foundation model that unifies diverse gaze-centric tasks for holistic gaze following. Benefiting from large-scale multi-task and cross-domain training, LookAnything flexibly adapts to various settings, generating diverse outputs (points, boxes, heatmaps, and language) and supporting broad gaze-centric localization, description, and reasoning. At its core, we introduce learnable gaze-prior queries to promote gaze-aware representation learning, eliminating the need for auxiliary external inputs. To facilitate this paradigm, we construct HoliGaze, a comprehensive corpus and benchmark comprising 311K question-answer pairs across 5 capability dimensions and 9 distinct tasks. Experiments demonstrate that LookAnything consistently outperforms 33 leading vision-language models on holistic gaze following, while remaining highly competitive with dedicated specialists across 5 conventional target detection benchmarks. Evaluation on unseen datasets and deployment on a real robot further validate its strong out-of-domain generalization and flexible adaptation in real-world scenarios.

title: LoomKV: Lossless KV Cache Compression from GPU Memory to SSD for LLM Serving
summary: Large language model (LLM) serving engines offload the key/value (KV) cache from GPU memory to host DRAM and SSD so multi-turn and agent requests can reuse prompt prefixes. Capacity then limits service at two levels: external tiers govern prefix reuse before eviction, while the GPU KV pool bounds concurrent long requests, and lossy compression alters KV values and outputs. LoomKV brings lossless KV compression to both external tiers (tier mode) and the GPU pool (pool mode) on an unmodified engine. Using a calibrated per-head two-level 3-bit code over BF16 high bytes (sign and upper seven exponent bits), LoomKV stores BF16 KV at 0.71 of its raw size across nine models and FP8 KV at 0.85-0.87. In tier mode, TileStream writes exact-length records with length readback off the load path, leaving tier storage, eviction, and prefetch unchanged, and decompresses fetched records straight into scattered GPU pages. In pool mode, FragPack packs variable-length records into smaller shared-budget GPU pages read in place by a fused decode-attention kernel faster than FlashAttention-3 on BF16. Built with LMCache and vLLM, LoomKV makes compressed tiers act as 1.4x larger raw tiers on AgentX: across LMCache's LRU cliff, tier mode delivers 2.7-3.6x raw's goodput and 1.9-3.1x lower mean time-to-first-token (TTFT), shifts the cliff identically under other simulated replacement policies, and cuts repeated-prompt TTFT up to 1.7x via SSD-to-DRAM promotion. When tiers hold the working set, pool mode fits 1.31-1.34x as many GPU tokens, admitting 12 long requests with roughly raw's queue and goodput at 8. On an AI IDE trace where both tiers and the GPU pool are constrained, tier and pool modes raise goodput by 1.24x and 1.59x. Where raw capacity suffices, compression costs at most 2.2% throughput; tier mode is bit-exact with raw tiers, and pool mode matches FlashAttention-3's numerical accuracy.

title: LoopDVR: Looped Transformer for Efficient Dense Visual Recognition
summary: We propose LoopDVR, a framework for converting pretrained Transformer-based dense visual recognition models into parameter-efficient looped networks. Rather than reducing the network width or depth directly, LoopDVR reuses Transformer blocks across layers in both the ViT backbone and Transformer decoder, reducing the number of parameters while retaining the original computational structure. However, naively sharing parameters can disrupt the distinct transformations learned at different depths. To address this challenge, we identify suitable sharing groups based on inter-layer representation dissimilarity and keep the final backbone block independent for multi-scale feature construction. We then initialize each shared backbone block with the pretrained weights of its group's terminal layer to better preserve the learned representations. An independent Loop Adapter at each layer further helps retain depth-specific transformations within shared blocks. Subsequently, we distill visual representations into the looped backbone and integrate it with a looped decoder for task-specific training. Experiments demonstrate that LoopDVR achieves the best accuracy--parameter trade-offs across dense recognition tasks. Compared with the reference models, it reduces parameters by approximately 28% while maintaining competitive accuracy. Notably, LoopDet-S achieves 50.9 box AP with only 7.0M parameters, highlighting its effectiveness in compact models.

title: LoopFit: Retrofitting Pretrained Diffusion Transformers with Recurrent Refinement
summary: Scaling inference computation offers a way to improve diffusion transformers (DiTs), but taking more sampling steps leaves the depth of each denoising prediction unchanged. Recurrently reusing Transformer blocks increases computation within each step, allowing further refinement of hidden representations. Retrofitting pretrained models enables this capability without repeating pretraining, but requires blocks learned for fixed-depth computation to refine states produced by their own repeated application. The challenge is to use each additional pass to correct local errors without disrupting the structure established by earlier passes. We introduce LoopFit, which uses feedback from earlier passes to guide refinement at each image patch. Residual Attention Modulation (RAM) uses each patch's feature change in one pass to scale and shift its input to attention in the next. During training, Residual Relay Loss (RRL) gives greater weight to patches whose prediction errors persist across passes. A noise-dependent depth schedule speeds up sampling by using four passes at high noise and one at lower noise levels. At comparable cost, backbones trained with four passes solve more problems using recurrent depth than extra sampling steps. Across 12 visual puzzle settings, LoopFit solves 89.8% of boards, compared with 87.8% for the strongest baseline evaluated on all 12. Most of the gain comes from tracing long paths on mazes and frozen lakes.

title: Loupe: Reinforcing Knowledge-Intensive Video Generation Agents
summary: Knowledge-intensive video generation remains challenging because prompts often omit the facts, appearances, and temporal relationships required for accurate generation. While search-based workflows can retrieve missing evidence, manually designed strategies limit adaptive planning, and conventional training suffers from costly video-level feedback and coarse trajectory-level credit assignment. In this paper, we present Loupe, a video generation agent that retrieves and verifies textual and visual evidence to construct evidence-grounded temporal video prompts with reference images. We further introduce Rubric-Based Credit (RBC), which leverages prompt-specific factual, visual, and temporal requirements to evaluate intermediate search and planning decisions before video rendering. Building on RBC, RBC-SFT reweights assistant-token learning by step quality, while RBC-GRPO incorporates step-level credits alongside a final planning reward, without rendering videos during RL. To address the lack of dedicated search-oriented evaluation, we construct Search-VBench, which contains 150 held-out prompts across seven categories. Experiments show that Loupe improves all four evaluation dimensions across three video generators, raising the overall score of MiniMax-H3 from 32.80 to 70.67 and outperforming an untrained search workflow. Ablation experiments show that full RBC training outperforms standard SFT followed by trajectory-level GRPO by 5.27 points. Human evaluations and results on Sci-VBench and KIVI-Bench further demonstrate improved generation quality, scientific grounding, factual precision, and helpfulness. Our project page is available at https://zengkaiya.github.io/Loupe/.

title: Lyris: Layout-Guided Long Video Generation with Persistent 3D Memory
summary: Exploring a scene from as little as a single photo requires generating a long, camera-controlled walkthrough that extends far beyond what was captured, yet remains consistent upon return. Memory-based video generation methods preserve what they have already seen, but have no anchor beyond it, where the camera drifts from its path and a text prompt can name objects but not place them. Layout-conditioned methods provide such an anchor and precise control over what appears where, but rely on layouts that are typically authored by hand. Both limitations arise because, beyond what was captured, nothing anchors the video model unless a human authors one. To overcome both, we propose Lyris, a long video generation framework that never leaves the video model without an anchor: a persistent point-cloud memory where the scene has been observed or generated, and a 3D layout that a vision-language model authors where it has not. Our key insight is that the interface between the two models can be surprisingly coarse. A layout of one labeled 3D box per object is simple enough for a vision-language model to author (and for a user to edit), yet expressive enough for a video model to follow once rendered along the camera path. We demonstrate walkthroughs of over three minutes and 50 meters from a single photo, passing through doorways into rooms it never shows. When evaluated on minute-long round trips across four datasets, Lyris outperforms state-of-the-art methods by a wide margin, reducing camera error by 3.8x and improving consistency upon return by 22% on average.

title: MAGPIE: Agentic Multi-Reference Image Generation via Executable Scene Construction
summary: Multi-reference image generation requires a model to preserve the appearance of selected subjects while arranging them according to an instruction. Despite recent progress in reference-based generation and compositional control, reliably organizing selected subjects into the intended scene remains challenging. Although existing methods provide various forms of compositional guidance, the planned relationships are not always explicitly instantiated for inspection and refinement before image synthesis. To address this limitation, we introduce MAGPIE, which represents the intended composition as a simplified 3D scene defined by an executable Blender program. A coding agent links each scene instance to its reference, checks the geometry and rendered view against the instruction, and revises the program to correct discrepancies. The final proxy rendering serves as a visual plan for the image generator. Using MAGPIE-Instruct-3K, we train the generator to follow this plan while drawing each subject's appearance from its reference. MAGPIE improves both Qwen and FLUX on DreamOmni2 and SconeEval. With FLUX, it improves overall success on DreamOmni2 by 28.21 percentage points over the original backbone and achieves the highest overall score among the models evaluated on SconeEval.

title: MELODI: Similarity-Identity Decoupling for Lightweight Ranking
summary: For latency-constrained candidate ranking, we propose a similarity-identity decoupling framework that separates target-history compatibility from target-only information. We study two orders for computing pooled similarity, similarity-then-pool and pool-then-similarity, and identify linearity of the similarity operator in its history argument, for each fixed target, as sufficient for their equivalence, justifying the cheaper pool-then-similarity form. We instantiate the framework as multi-head efficient lightweight operator for decoupling identity and similarity (MELODI), whose similarity branch combines target-conditioned multi-head history pooling with a single residual-free cross layer that is linear in its pooled-history input and whose identity branch is problem-dependent. On public benchmark datasets, MELODI matches or surpasses the evaluated target-aware and target-agnostic baselines. On two large-scale industrial datasets, its area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC), normalised discounted cumulative gain (NDCG), and recall values are equal to or higher than those of the evaluated target-aware baselines. Processor measurements show lower latency than the evaluated candidate-conditioned baselines at large candidate counts, further reduced by request-local history reuse.

title: MESSI: Multi-Expert Soccer Skill Integration for Physics-Based Character Control
summary: Physics-based soccer characters must perform diverse motor skills and transition smoothly between them, such as dribbling into a shot. However, skills that perform well in isolation may fail when executed sequentially, as preceding behaviors can leave the character and ball in unfamiliar states. We present MESSI (Multi-Expert Soccer Skill Integration), a framework that enables multiple soccer skill transitions through shared adaptation while preserving the original skill policy outside transitions. MESSI first trains eight task-competent experts using motion priors and task rewards, then distills them into a unified, skill-conditioned Transformer. Rather than retraining individual experts for different transitions, we train a shared, context-conditioned low-rank adapter on the frozen student through online reinforcement learning. Activated upon skill switching, the adapter helps the target skill handle unfamiliar entry states, while a learned exit mechanism determines when to return control to the original student. By disabling the adapter during native skill execution, MESSI preserves the original student policy by construction. Experiments across individual skills, skill transitions, and continuous skill chains demonstrate substantial improvements over direct switching, including an increase in dribbling-to-shooting success from 19.8% to 61.8%.

title: MIFLOW: Dynamic Recent-Behavior Priors for Reference-Calibrated Online Flow-Policy Reinforcement Learning
summary: Flow-based policies provide expressive action distributions for continuous-control reinforcement learning. In online actor-critic learning, off-policy value estimates can be unreliable in poorly covered action regions, where expressive policies may shift probability mass toward critic-favored actions. We propose MIFLOW, which calibrates online flow-policy learning with a recency-adaptive flow-matching prior fitted to recently executed actions. Inspired by canalization as a qualitative analogy for path-dependent stabilization, we use the prior as a moving density reference for value-guided policy improvement. MIFLOW uses the approximate recent-action log-density in a dimension-normalized correction to both actor updates and critic targets. This correction increases the cost of low-density actions while keeping them available. Across six MuJoCo continuous-control tasks and five random seeds, MIFLOW achieves competitive mean return curves and higher late-training mean returns than the evaluated baselines on several tasks. In a Walker2d-v4 case study, MIFLOW shows a lower proportion of actions assigned low density by the learned reference, both overall and among high-Q actions. Prior-family and prior-buffer comparisons show task-dependent differences in returns and prior-defined diagnostics. These results support dynamic recent-behavior priors for reference calibration in the evaluated settings. The diagnostics measure how sampled actions align with the learned reference. True action support and critic extrapolation error remain unmeasured in these experiments.

title: MOSAIC: Memory-Organized Search with Anti-Imitation Crossover for Training-Free Microarchitecture Optimization
summary: Large language models can generate cache-replacement policies. The central challenge is to retain performance on workloads excluded from the search. In our adaptations of published search methods, generated code resembles established policies, with cosine similarities of 0.78-0.84. The wider comparison also shows held-out harmonic-mean instructions-per-cycle (IPC) losses of 1.0-2.4%. We present MOSAIC, a search controller that improves policies without updating language-model weights. It stores concise lessons from previous evaluations rather than repeatedly copying high-scoring code. When improvement stops, it selects two high-scoring policies whose code embeddings differ and asks the model to combine their mechanisms. Novelty prompts and model rotation support this search; controlled memory edits test how the stored lessons affect later proposals. We evaluate cache replacement using intervention-level cross-validation and a wider comparison on ten memory-intensive SPEC2006 workloads. MOSAIC reaches a 51.1% peak hit rate on the primary search workload and a 47.9% held-out mean in the intervention study. Removing crossover reduces these values by 7.8 and 21.8 percentage points, respectively, whereas the tested stronger model improves the held-out mean by 0.4 points. In the wider IPC comparison, MOSAIC has the smallest held-out gap (0.31%) and the highest held-out IPC among the evaluated LLM configurations. Adapting the same controller to data prefetching gives a 4.8% mean speedup over the LRU reference configuration. The accompanying corpus contains 10,687 generated policies with lineage and per-iteration prompt logs.

title: MSW: a Multi-Scale Sliced Wasserstein Distance Between Image Distributions
summary: We propose the multi-scale sliced Wasserstein (MSW) distance between image distributions, which operates in pixel space and requires no trained network. MSW convolves images with a fixed bank of discrete cosine filters at several scales, pools the responses over all positions, and compares the resulting one-dimensional distributions using the Wasserstein distance. We pair MSW with an exact two-sample test that gives calibrated p-values. Most metrics compare two image sets in the latent space of a pretrained network. We show that these metrics are insensitive to simple perturbations of the images, because the latent space is nearly invariant to them. In contrast, MSW detects smaller perturbations than latent-space metrics and needs far fewer images to do so. Although it uses no learned features, it still detects semantic changes of the image distribution. Finally, MSW matches or outperforms existing Wasserstein-based metrics in our experiments.

title: MXFP4 for LLM Inference: Complementary Post-Training Quantization Techniques and Their Interactions
summary: Recent advances in low-precision representation have introduced several microscaling numerical formats for LLM quantization.
